speechtext:
The House resumed from Monday, December 11, 1989, consideration of the motion of Mr. Althouse:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should consider the advisability of introducing measures to amend the Western Grain Stabilization Act to include coverage for producers who feed their own grain to their livestock; and the amendment of Mr. Funk:
That the motion be amended by adding immediately after the words "Western Grain Stabilization Act" the following:
"and Agricultural Stabilization Act'.

maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   AGRICULTURE WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to speak in support of the motion of my colleague, the hon. member for Mackenzie and the amendment of my colleague, the hon. member for Prince Albert-Churchill River on the matter of making it possible for farmers to be covered under the Western Grain Stabilization Act or the Agricultural Stabilization Act for grain that they grew and fed to their own livestock, particularly cattle and hogs.
I have read in Hansard what members from all parties had to say during the debate. I must say that I found those who spoke, in the main from the government side, did all kinds of talking around the subject matter, but did not examine what it is that the agricultural industry wants and for what has been asking for a long time.
One must remind the House that the following support this kind of move: the Canadian Pork Council, the Ontario Federation of Agriculture, the Ontario Cattlemen's Association, the chicken producers, the egg producers marketing board, milk marketing board, pork producers marketing board, sheep marketing agency, turkey producers, the three prairie wheat pools, and the UPA of the province of Quebec which is probably the largest farm organization in all of Canada, as well as many groups and individuals.
In March 1988, Mr. Kraft, a University of Manitoba economist, in his study on income stabilization and eligibility of farm-fed grain recommended that either the WGS or the red meat stabilization formula could accommodate farm-fed grain. The policy choices would be to change the grains programs to a production based qualification from the current marketing qualifications, or to modify the red meat stabilization formula to account for the costs of producing grain rather than just buying grain.
It makes no sense to allow the farmer full credit for the cost of the grain he purchased from a neighbour, feed grain dealer, or the Canadian Wheat Board. He is covered for the full cost of that, but he is not covered for the cost of grain he raises on his own farm and feeds to his hogs or cattle. That is something worse even than an anomaly. It would seem to me that that is totally unfair.
Let me quote from a letter from the Canadian Pork Council dated September 22, 1988, which states:
It is our view that grain should be treated no differently if it happens to be marketed through a livestock operation on the same farm rather than sold through commercial channels, which can include sales to other domestic livestock operations. All grain, whether immediately sold or fed to livestock, incurs the same basic costs. Growing grain and feeding hogs, for example, should be regarded as distinctly separate activities just as feeding hogs and feeding cattle within the same enterprise structure are treated as being unconnected for purposes of stabilization coverage for either of these two commodities.
The letter further states:

February 12, 1990
Private Members' Business
The Canadian Pork Council is advocating that immediate steps be
taken to correct this inequity, and to include farm-fed grain in all
current (which includes programs for the 1986-87 and the 1987-88
crops) and future grain stabilization programs.
In eastern Canada, grain produced and consumed on farms equals total sales off the farm and in western Canada it represents 20 per cent of all production. That is a lot of grain.
Excluding the farm-fed grain from qualifying under the Agricultural Stabilization Act or the Western Grain Stabilization Act, and not accounting for grain production costs in the red meat stabilization programs, has removed a portion of farm income derived from farm-fed grain from the farm income stabilization programs.
The policy choices to include the farm-fed component in stabilization are either to change the grain programs to a production based qualification from the marketing qualifications, or modify the red meat stabilization formula to account for the costs of producing grain rather than just buying feed grain. The policy change requires either the grains or the red meat stabilization programs be modified, but not both.
I know it was alleged that some cattle or hog producers would be collecting twice. We submit that it is done under one program or the other, but not both.
A production based grain stabilization program would require farmers to register the land producing each crop. The land must be assigned at productivity rating and stabilization payments would be triggered whenever the moving average support level of income was not attained.
Stabilization income levels would change from year to year because of crop prices and operation costs, but they would not be related to current crop yields or sales. Participants in a crop production based stabilization program would pay a premium when it was due. They would pay the premium when they were registering their land and their crop base.
Pay-out support levels would be dependent upon the premiums and contributions from government. All grain and oilseeds for which sufficient information on yields, prices and costs exist, should qualify for the production based programs.
Much of the information required for a crop production based stabilization program is currently used and processed by the provincial crop insurance corporations. Administration of crop production based stabilization programs would merely extend the responsibilities of the crop insurance administration rather than change the nature of their work.
In fact, I have long felt that the provincial crop insurance programs, and there are a few federal programs, should be integrated so that there would only be one administration cost. It would probably be a quicker and more efficient treatment of the producers who are supposed to benefit.
Incorporating grain production costs into the red meat stabilization formula could be accomplished by either having two formulae or one with a weighted average which recognizes the share of grain produced and fed on farms. The two-formula approach recognizes that some livestock operations purchase most of their feed requirements while others produce their own feed. The two-formula approach allows the participants to elect which procedure best represents their cost structure.
The motion of my hon. friend for Mackenzie corrects what I consider to be more than an anomaly. It is unfair. I would hope that all members, in the desire that we all have to do more about stabilizing and enlarging the income of our agricultural producers, would be anxious to pass this motion which only asks the government to "consider", and does not require the government to do anything. It gives them a sense of what the House of Commons feels, that they should consider what the motion of my hon. friend says, then the government could reply and report back to the House of Commons.
I hope that all members will support both the amendment and the motion submitted by the hon. member for Mackenzie.

maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   AGRICULTURE WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity to enter this debate. The issue which we are discussing is certainly an important one. Farm-fed grain plays a significant role in our agriculture economy. About half of Canada's cereal crops, with the exception of wheat, are fed to livestock. The promotion of farm-fed grains is even higher in the



February 12, 1990

maritimes. There, even when wheat is included, about 30 per cent of the crops are fed on farms.
Farmers across the country are concerned because the role which farm-fed grain plays in the agricultural economy is not acknowledged in stabilization programs. In some livestock support programs, the price of grain is included in the formula for triggering payments. Therefore, when grain prices go up, support prices for livestock go up.
Livestock support programs do not take the cost of producing farm-fed grain into account. If the price of grain stays the same but grain production costs increase, the high cost of growing grain is not reflected in payments through livestock support programs.
This is an important issue, but it cannot be considered in isolation. Right now, the federal government is undertaking an extensive review of all agricultural policies and programs in consultation with farm organizations and the provinces. The way that farm-fed grain is included in the farm safety net must be discussed in the broad context of that policy review.
At first glance, including farm-fed grain in the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the Agricultural Stabilization Act seems like a simple way to provide income protection for farmers who feed grain to their livestock. Let us take a closer look at the issue. Changing the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the Agricultural Stabilization Act to include farm-fed grain has a number of implications for both grain and livestock farmers.
First of all, some programs already include part of the costs of producing farm-fed grain. The dairy program is one example. If farm-fed grain were included in the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the Agricultural Stabilization Act, some farmers would be compensated twice for the same grain.
This was a point which the Standing Committee on Agriculture emphasized in its January, 1986 report on the Western Grain Stabilization Act. The committee concluded:
It should be only for the final products marketed that the producer receives market protection under the Western Grain Stabilization Act or the Agricultural Stabilization Act. In the case of livestock producers, they face the livestock market but not the grain market risk. Treating livestock producers as grain producers means the grain may be covered in the raw form and again as it goes into the final product.
Private Members' Business
That is what the committee stated. Beyond that, including farm-fed grain in the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the Agricultural Stabilization Act would mean changing the fundamental structure of these programs. Rather than being based on commercial sales, the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the Agricultural Stabilization Act would be based on production. If that were the case, the administration would have to collect yield data on every single farmer enrolled in the program. That would be a costly and impractical exercise.
In many cases, the information simply does not exist, so payments would have to be based on a regional yield average. Most farmers find this unacceptable. Farmers with yields below the regional average would be overpaid and those with higher yields would be underpaid.
Changing the basis on which payments are made could result in trading off the interests of one commodity group against the other.
Although including farm-fed grain in the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the Agricultural Stabilization Act would mean more protection for livestock farmers, it would remove the protection for grain farmers which these programs were designed to provide. Both the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the Agricultural Stabilization Act are designed to protect producers from a dramatic loss of income when they are unable to make sales.
For example, right now the Western Grain Stabilization Act is based on sales. If producers cannot make delivery, that is reflected in reduced sales and a Western Grain Stabilization Act payment can be triggered. If the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the Agricultural Stabilization Act were based on production, payments under both programs might not be triggered because of a drop in deliveries.
As a last point, including farm-fed grain in the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the Agricultural Stabilization Act would make both programs more expensive and farmers would end up footing the bill along with the federal government.
The way in which farm-fed grain is included in stabilization programs must be addressed through a comprehensive safety net program. At the national agri-food conference in December, the Minister of Agriculture announced that the National Grains Bureau

February 12, 1990
Private Members' Business
would lead the consultations with industry and the provinces on developing a grain safety net program.
The committee on grain safety nets had its first meeting in January and is expected to present a proposal for consideration by agricultural ministers in the spring. Legislation should be in place by the end of the year.
We need to develop a stabilization program which will do three things: first, it must respond to the needs of the producers; second, it must have a sound financial base; and finally, it must be based on a fair cost-sharing arrangement among farmers and provincial and federal governments.
Responding to the needs of farmers means putting a program in place in which farmers make long-term plans for their operations. In recent years, the federal government has responded to declines in farm income and production with ad hoc assistance. Farmers needed that assistance. However, relying on ad hoc programs makes it difficult for farmers to manage their operations effectively.
During the national agri-food policy conference, the Minister of Agriculture announced that a government-industry task force would be set up to look at several aspects of farm management. These include the special needs of beginning farmers, the management tools farmers need, the role of lending institutions, and the effectiveness of subsidized interest rates.
Over the next six months, options will be developed in consultation with industry. Federal and provincial ministers of agriculture will look at these options at their final meeting in August, 1990. Public consultations will start in the fall.
The issue of how farm-fed grain should be included in agricultural stabilization programs is an important one. It is an issue which must be considered in the context of over-all policy review. As part of the policy review, both levels of government and the industry are now in the process of developing options for grain safety net programs. The committee on grain safety nets held its first meeting in January and will be discussing several options with the industry over the winter. By late spring the committee is expected to have recommendations to be considered by ministers and legislation will be in place by the fall.
The way in which farm-fed grain is included in grain safety nets will be discussed in the context of the over-all safety net review. I have spoken briefly about the implications of adding farm-fed grain to existing grain stabilization programs. Simply adding farm-fed grain to the Western Grain Stabilization Act or the Agricultural Stabilization Act would likely create more inequities than it would solve. That is why the issue must be discussed in the context of the overall grain safety net review. I am confident that working with farmers and with the province we can arrive at a safety net program which will satisfy the needs of farmers and their livestock industry.

maintopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   AGRICULTURE WESTERN GRAIN STABILIZATION ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted to participate in this debate.
I listened with interest to the remarks of my colleague from across the way. He enumerated several problems that will occur the motion if the motion is adopted. Let me repeat that the motion asks the government to consider the advisability of introducing measures to amend the Western Grain Stabilization Act to include coverage for producers who feed their grain to their livestock. The key word here is that the government should consider the advisability.
We are asking the government to study and recognize that a problem exists now. Producers of red meat products who grow their own feed and grain are in a disadvantaged position compared to those producers who purchase their feed. The system discriminates, perhaps unconsciously, against one type of producer compared to his neighbour.
Theoretically, there are ways around this. Neighbours could start selling the grains they grow to each other but I do not think we want to encourage any more games to be played. Often when I go into the rural area of my constituency farmers tell me that it is not enough to know the ins and outs of growing a crop. Now they have to become experts at the various government programs. These anomalies in the existing program and legislation are forcing farmers to become like high-priced tax accountants in order to learn how to play the system.
Our motion asks the government to first recognize the problem and then give some commitments to working with members of the House and members of the agricultural community to find ways and means by which we can
February 12, 1990

solve the problems that we are facing. In a nutshell, that is the purpose of the motion.
I appeal to members of the government to support our motion. It is not a motion that condemns the government in any way. I believe it is a motion that government members should have no difficulty supporting because it is presented in the spirit of trying to improve agriculture in this country and help our farmers. I hope that government members will see it as such and will support the motion.
Let me also say just a few words about the state of agriculture back home. During the Christmas break I visited many of the rural communities in my riding of Regina-Qu'Appelle.
I had the time to go into the local cafes, to sit in the booths, to drink gallons of coffee, and to talk with members of the farming community, people from the small towns I was visiting. I must say that I have never experienced such a psychological depression as what exists in rural Saskatchewan today. There is a sense of hopelessness, a sense of helplessness, a sense that nobody out there is listening to their concerns, let alone being able to do anything about it.
I find the type of fatalism that exists out there today extremely saddening. I talked with young farmers who were working land that had belonged to their family for generations. They have a sense of hopelessness and just shrugged their shoulders and said: "Well, Mr. de Jong, what can I do any more? We are totally in debt. We are totally uncertain as to what types of government programs and types of assistance there will be to keep us on the land".
I was shown old newspaper articles with the cost of wheat 10 or 20 years ago. In fact it is not much higher today and in many cases even lower. The cost of production in the last decade or two has soared. There is a sense that it is just not going to work any more. They wonder why they are out there struggling, trying to make ends meet, when they see no light at the end of the tunnel. This Parliament has must address those problems.
In conclusion, the farming community needs some help. It needs help from this Parliament. It needs some understanding and co-operation in developing policies of
Private Members' Business
mutual interest so that the farming community in this country will not go down the drain.
Accepting this resolution is a small but significant indication to our farmers that this Parliament is interested in their concerns and will rise above our partisan interests. The effort by my colleagues who have moved this motion is an effort of co-operation with the government to find a solution to this problem. I hope the government will accept it and, in doing so, will send out a signal to the farmers that this Parliament is willing to work together to find solutions to their problems.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I pleased to speak to the motion this afternoon. We are all aware of the problems Canadian grain farmers face. The financial squeeze which began gripping farmers in the middle of the decade has not yet loosened. Export subsidy battles fought by others on the world grain markets have depressed the prices Canadian farmers get for their grain. Until there is some further progress made in the trade talks through the GATT, or unless there are production problems in major grain growing regions, the situation will remain uncertain.
In recent years dealing with problems brought on by low commodity prices has meant relying to a large extent on ad hoc government programs for support. In 1986 and 1987 the federal government provided farmers with a total of $2.1 billion through the Special Canadian Grains Program. In 1988 the Canadian Crop Drought Assistance Program paid out $850 million to farmers who suffered crop losses because of the severe drought.
We cannot continue to rely on ad hoc government assistance. There must be a better way in place to provide protection to grain and oilseed producers. This government has set out to find that better way. It began last year with changes to crop insurance plans. Coverage was increased in 1989. As a result of that increased coverage the revamped crop insurance programs in 1989 provided farmers with more coverage than in the previous year.
For example, the 1988 crop insurance payments for wheat on stubble in Saskatchewan ranged from about $32 to $53 an acre, depending on the risk area. In 1989, coverage for the same risk areas ranged from about $50 to $85 per acre.

February 12, 1990
Private Members' Business
In 1988, a southeastern Saskatchewan fanner, who grew a crop of wheat on summer fallow would have been eligible for about $60 an acre in crop insurance. On top of this, the same farmer would also have received about $14 an acre from the Canadian Crop Drought Assistance Program. The maximum coverage for that farmer would have been approximately $75 an acre.
After changes to crop insurance in 1989, that same farmer would have been eligible for about $94 an acre from crop insurance alone. Producers in Alberta and Manitoba were also eligible for more coverage through crop insurance alone in 1989 than they were able to collect from drought assistance and crop insurance in 1988.
The changes to crop insurance protection was a first step. Now this government is moving on the development of a national safety net program for all grain and oilseed producers. It seems inappropriate at this time to be tinkering with individual programs like the WGSA and the ASA. We have to look at this issue in a broader context.
At the National Agri-Food Policy Conference in Ottawa in December, it was agreed there is an urgent need to help develop a national safety net program that is fair to all grain and oilseed producers. Work on this issue is being undertaken as part of the federal government's national agricultural policy review. It was announced at the conference that the national grains bureau in Winnipeg would take the lead in working to develop a national grain safety net program.
This task will include the involvement of provincial governments and those industry representatives in developing a proposal. Meetings are under way this month. It is expected that a proposal should be ready by late spring with enabling legislation developed by December 1990.
The federal government is moving quickly on this issue. The farm income problems projected for the next year must be taken into account. There is also a need to ensure that action taken now is in line with the longer term goals as safety nets are developed for all farmers.
Part of the review, of course, is the examination of existing safety net programs. The advisory committee of the western grain stabilization program has been asked
to examine issues surrounding the potential transition of the WGSA to a more comprehensive safety net program.
This government is moving on the issue. In fact, progress has been made. The existing federal-provincial working group on safety nets is continuing the work it began in 1988. Its key objective is to develop a long term comprehensive safety net policy for all commodities and all farmers.
A series of regional meetings were held during 1988 among all farm leaders across Canada and government to help identify the problems which exist with existing safety net programs and determine the direction that would be taken for agriculture in the future.
Subsequently, the National Grains Bureau in Winnipeg developed a number of grain safety options which were presented to farm leaders. The work of the National Grains Bureau on safety nets is continuing. Continued discussion with farm leaders across Canada with other government members is continuing to work out a program for agriculture. As a government we are working out a comprehensive program which is fair to all producers across Canada. It will have a sound financial base for Canadian farmers which they require at this time.
This government has taken action and will continue to take action to ensure that agriculture is protected across this great land. We feel that it is appropriate for this government to continue to discuss with the farm leaders the future of agriculture, combining crop insurance and some safety net programs. We are continuing working with that to develop protection for producers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak briefly on the motion that is before us from the NDP. I would just like to make a few comments and explain to the House an experience that I had last Friday which I think is indicative of the situation that we have in the agriculture community at the present time.
Last Friday I took the opportunity to attend one of the largest, if not the largest, farm machinery equipment shows in Canada that takes place each year in February in Toronto. From my previous experience as an active farmer-producer I met many acquaintances there who were manning the booths for the dealerships that were there. They said that the attendance at the show was excellent. That was quite evident on Friday when I was there. However, they said that they found this year probably without question the worst year as far as
February 12, 1990

interest from producers is concerned. They were there to look.
On the lighter side, I can never forget my father saying that that was an excellent place to go once a year because you could see a lot of things that you could get along without. It is like going to a sportsman's show or whatever, and you could go home and appreciate what you did have at home.
They said it was very depressing that those farmer producers were simply not interested. They simply do not feel confident with the industry that they are involved in. They have seen many things happening. The interest free provision of the advance payment for crops removed. It was a management tool that they have used.
The basic improvements to the crop insurance bill are all well and good, but they are saying that because there has not been a tripartite type of program put in place with a three-way split on the premiums that the risks are going up and the premiums are going to be so high for that extra extent on the risk that they are probably not going to be able to afford it. They will be no better off than they were in the past.
There is a problem out there and I feel that this motion is a good one. It is simply asking the government to consider those improvements. I ask the members opposite to vote in the true spirit of this motion and not oppose it just because it came from a party on this side of the House. The motion seeks nothing specific. I can tell you from past experience that the way the stabilization act works now is not fair.
A farmer who produces his own grain for consumption by his own herd of cattle or hogs is not able to take part in the stabilization program because he has to subtract what he purchased from what he sold. There is no net benefit.
However, if a farmer is the sole producer of grain, he can take part in the stabilization program. If he is a purchaser of feeds, he cannot benefit from that. What I am saying is that whether I sell as a primary producer, whether I sell to the local grain elevator, my own grain enterprise in my farming operation, my hog enterprise or
Private Members' Business
my beef producing enterprise, a sale should be a sale no matter which way it goes.
At the present time the program is not fair. This motion requests that the government consider this and rather than take something away from producers, make an improvement to it. The producers are eager and willing to sit down with the government and make those suggestions.
The tripartite program is the type of program that can be protected and explained in other countries so that it is not challenged under the free trade agreement, as it has been, and we are going to have to work hard in order to do that.
In summary, I am requesting the government to vote in the spirit of this House and support this bill. The motion is asking the government to sit down and discuss this situation for the betterment of the industry which so many Canadians are involved in.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to join this debate today on this important agricultural topic.
The issue of iftcluding farm-fed grain in stabilization programs is a very important one. It is an issue that cannot be considered in isolation. Including farm-fed grain in stabilization programs must be looked at in the broad context of all agricultural stabilization programs.
As you know, the federal government is undertaking a major review of all agricultural policies and programs. Any changes to the Western Grain Stabilization Program and the Agricultural Stabilization Program will be considered in the context of that review.
No farmer would want to make a decision about what he or she was going to plant on a quarter section without an understanding of the broader context of the future of that farm. I suggest that members of the House should keep that in mind. This government is looking at the over-all strategy and the whole Canadian farm sector before making a specific decision about one aspect of it.
The first step in the review process was the release of the discussion paper "Growing Together" last November 7. In that paper the federal government identified four pillars on which our vision for agriculture rests. They are market responsiveness, greater self-reliance in the agri-

February 12, 1990
Private Members' Business
food sector, a national policy which recognizes regional diversity and increased environmental sustainability.
The next step was the national agri-food policy conference in Ottawa in December. Over 1,800 people representing farmers, processors, consumers and other groups with a stake in the agricultural industry attended that conference.
During the policy conference a series of panel discussions on seven key issues were held. Now we are in the process of following up on those discussions. Task forces have been established in a number of areas, including market development and value-added, farm finance and management, safety nets, supply management, transportation, food safety and sustainable agriculture.
This is how farm safety nets fit into that over-all global picture. A federal-provincial working group on farm safety nets was in place before the policy review started last fall. That group will continue its work. Their objective is to develop a long-term comprehensive safety net program for all commodities and for all farmers. The group will prepare an interim report to be given to federal and provincial agricultural ministers at their annual meeting. In the fall of this year the group will consult with farm groups and other interested parties.
In addition to the working group on farm safety nets a special, committee has been established to look specifically at the question of grain safety nets. The committee was established after the policy conference in December. It has been set up because this government recognizes that grain and oilseeds farmers are likely to face some veiy serious income problems in the coming year.
We need to develop proposals to assist these farmers immediately. These proposals must fit within a national program framework. The Minister of Agriculture has asked the National Grains Bureau to lead the consultation with industry and with the provinces. That process is already under way. The committee had its first meeting in Winnipeg during the second week of January. That committee is expected to present a proposal to ministers for a grain safety net program by late spring. Proposed legislation should be submitted by the end of the year.
This is where the issue we are discussing today fits in. If we are going to make changes in the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the Agriculture Stabilization Act then we must consider these changes in the context of the review of grain safety nets and of all farm safety nets which is taking place now.
Including farm-fed grain and stabilization programs is a longstanding and significant issue for farmers all across the country. The cost of producing grain to feed livestock is not fully taken into account in livestock stabilization programs or in grain income stabilization programs.
The member for Regina-Qu'Appelle asked the government to consider specific changes to the WGSA and the ASA. Looking at the whole picture of agriculture, this government is considering adaptations necessary to face the future in all aspects of agriculture. Growing Together is not just a question of making speeches, it is a commitment to agriculture, a commitment to producers and a commitment to people in the agri-food sector to take action over the course of the next year or two.
We invite the opposition to participate in that process in a constructive manner. Simply including farm-fed grain in the WGSA and the ASA may not be the best answer. In fact, taking this step could create a whole new set of inequities and perhaps a return to the business of ad hoc government programs. We need to have a sense of the over-all context.
First of all, some stabilization programs such as the dairy program already include the cost of farm-fed grain. If these costs were included in WGSA and ASA some producers would be overcompensated. Second, including farm-fed grain in WGSA and ASA would make a fundamental change in the basis of these programs. Right now both of these programs are based on commercial sales. If farm-fed grain were included in both programs then these programs would have to be based on production rather than on sales. This would add a whole new dimension to the administration of these programs.
Members opposite might want to increase the administrative burden for farmers and the administrative cost to taxpayers. I can assure you that members on this side do not. If both programs were based on production, the administration would have to collect yield data for individual farmers. In many cases this information simply would not be available. Both WGSA and ASA would have to be administered on the basis of regional yields. I
February 12, 1990

do not have to remind members of the difficulties we ran into when we established the recent drought assistance program on that sort of basis.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday's release of Nelson Mandela was an occasion for world-wide rejoicing. Having spent 28 years in prison for leading South Africa's black national movement, Mr. Mandela personally became a symbol of the terrible injustices inherent in his country's white supremacy laws.
In South Africa, as in nations of eastern Europe, we have witnessed events in recent weeks that many felt could not occur in our lifetime. Much credit must go to President de Klerk who has demonstrated an enlightened outlook and the courage to accelerate change. Yesterday did not by any means mean the end of apartheid, but it was, we must hope and pray, the beginning toward the end of this abhorrent system.

What we have, and the hon. member is very much aware of this, is a trade war that is going on between the European Community and the United States of America. The European Community has been engaged in huge subsidization of grain and oilseeds. It has changed from

becoming a major importer of grains to becoming the world's second largest exporter of grains. It has done it largely through the use of subsidies that have distorted world markets.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I wish to bring to the attention of the House a ruling on a question which hon. members will remember was raised by the hon. member for Calgary West on Wednesday, January 24, following several recorded divisions that day. Put simply, there was the suggestion that some hon. members may have voted twice.
Subsequently, these incidents were raised by the hon. member for Calgary West. The hon. member claimed, as a question of privilege, that contrary to the established rules and practices of this House, two members voted twice on those divisions. This charge was denied by the members involved, both on Wednesday when the issue was first raised, and again on Thursday.
The issue was extensively discussed last Thursday and I wish to thank all hon. members who made presentations.
On Friday, the hon. member for Windsor-St. Clair offered an apology to the House for any unintended misunderstandings caused by his actions during the divisions in question. This apology closes the matter in so far as the question of privilege is concerned.

However, as Speaker, I want to make a few comments on the events that took place. It is accepted practice that when the House is considering an item of government policy that is highly contentious, members of the opposition will seek to use any means available to them to delay the proceedings. As we have witnessed over the years the ingenuity of the opposition to find ways to delay the business of government is considerable. Such dilatory tactics, are of course, an important part of the adversarial nature of this place and a legitimate tool for the opposition. At the same time, however, I must point out that any such tactics by the opposition must fall squarely within the rules or practices of the House and I would ask all Hon. Members to keep this in mind.

At no time should dilatory tactics ever detract from the authority or the dignity of the House. In the heat of the moment, members may sometimes depart from the normal courtesies, but the basic respect for our practices must be insisted upon. The Chair would be derelict in its

February 12, 1990

duties to all hon. members and to this institution if it were to tolerate any erosion of that respect.
Therefore, I urge members on all sides of the House to consider their behaviour carefully, and most especially, in the heat of partisan debate in order that we may preserve and protect the dignity and respect due to this Chamber in which we have all been called to serve.
I thank hon. members for their interventions.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF AT AND EAST PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to bring to your attention a matter which I feel is a contempt of Parliament. It deals with Bill C-26, commonly referred to as the at and east program. I believe the action taken by Transport Canada and the Minister of Transport have usurped Parliament and in so doing have impeded the House in the performance of its function in respect of Bill C-26.
I propose very briefly to outline the relevant facts and state why I feel that a contempt of this House has been committed.
In last year's budget, it was announced that the at and east program would be eliminated effective July 15,1989. This program is found in Section 281 of the Railway Act which provides a subsidy to railways that are hauling grain and flour to eastern ports, mainly Saint John and Halifax, provided certain conditions are met. This program has been in effect for 20 years and in fact a whole economy has been built up in the maritimes around this program.
First reading of Bill C-26 took place on June 16, 1989 and since then the bill has not seen the light of day in this House until today. In the meantime, a series of moves by Transport Canada have, in effect, eliminated this program. This started with a meeting held on May 4, 1989, by officials of Transport Canada. That meeting was confirmed in a letter to myself from the Minister of Transport in which he states, and I quote:
On May 4, 1989, Transport Canada officials held a meeting in
Ottawa with representatives from affected organizations to provide
information on the decision.
This was followed by correspondence from Mr. C. McElman, Director of Rail Freight Programs with Transport Canada. This correspondence discusses the removal of this program.
As a result of this meeting, correspondence and other discussions, both CP Rail and CN Rail stopped hauling grain and flour pursuant to this section. This was confirmed, first of all, by letter from CP Rail on September 22, 1989. It states:

Privilege
By letter dated June 27,1989, Mr. McElman replied that the grain must be loaded in a railway car at an inland point on or before July 15, 1989 to be eligible for subsidy. Mr. McElman's reply confirmed the budget speech of the Minister of Finance.
In a further letter dated June 29, 1989, Mr. McElman again confirmed the demise of the At and East rates, when he stated, in part, that the rates and subsidy program are cancelled on the dates specified, even if Parliamentary approval comes at a later date.
A letter from CN Rail on December 13 confirms the same thing. It states: "CN has effectively cancelled certain provisions of Thriff-as they apply to the movement of grain in bulk and of flour for export".
This initiative is directly related to information provided by Mr. C. McElman of Transport Canada who clearly stated to the industry that even if parliamentary sanction was to be received at a later date, the rates and subsidy program would disappear on July 15, 1989.
How is this contempt of Parliament? In referring to your order of October 10-and I am paraphrasing-I believe a number of authorities have indicated that any act or omission which obstructs or impedes either House of Parliament in the performance of its function could well be contempt.
Mr. Speaker, in paraphrasing your words, also any act that has the effect or tends to diminish the authority of the House in the eyes of the public may well be contempt.
I believe this has happened with this bill and that this House will now be impeded in dealing with Bill C-26. This happened in two fashions: first of all, by the actions of Transport Canada and the Minister of Transport, as I have just outlined, and second, the fact that the bill has not been back in this House for seven months since the removal of this program. In fact, it has not been in the House since this program has been removed de facto. This has had a major effect on certain regions of the maritimes, particularly in Saint John, New Brunswick and Halifax, Nova Scotia.
I believe that the matter hinges, to some extent, on the fact that the bill is retroactive. I want to make it very clear that there is no dispute that bills can be retroactive. That is very clear. If, in fact, this bill passes this House, it will be good law. However, it is submitted that there is a need to be reasonable with this type of legislation.
Professor Hogg, who is one of the country's leading constitutional experts discusses this in the second edition of his book on constitutional law. On page 776, he states:
The power to enact retroactive laws, if exercised with appropriate restraint, is a proper tool of modem government.
But he stresses "appropriate restraint".
I think that also has to be considered in light of your ruling, Your Honour, on October 10, in which you stated at page 4461 of Hansard:
I expect the Department of Finance and other departments to study this ruling carefully and remind everyone within the Public Service that we are a parliamentary democracy, not a so-called executive democracy, nor a so-called administrative democracy.
I am concerned about the period since Transport Canada effectively removed Bill C-26 as it now stands drafted. What authority does Transport Canada have to make such an implementation? I think none. Only Parliament can enact or change legislation. Although we must be flexible, cabinet does not make the laws in this country, nor do departments. We are not in an executive or administrative democracy. If we are, why do we have Parliament at all? Surely there must be a role for parliamentarians to play in this country. If it is not the case, maybe we should all go home.
Mr. Speaker, unlike the GST which was referred to in your ruling on October 10, this is not something that will happen. It is something that already has happened. Already rail grain shipments have stopped to Halifax and Saint John, the elevator at Saint John has announced it will be closing at the end of February, the Halifax elevator is in trouble and Dover Flour Mills in Halifax is suffering. It is estimated that this is going to cost the maritimes some $27 million annually along with some 250 jobs. It is already happening because of an executive or administrative decision, not because of any act of this Parliament.
If Parliament should decide to leave the at and east or make any modifications, it may be too late because, as I said, already the elevator at Saint John is closed and this whole infrastructure that has developed around this program is being dismantled. The bill was introduced in June, the program was eliminated in July and it is only now that the bill is coming before Parliament.
In summary, there are two reasons for contempt today. First of all, that this bill is going beyond convention and historical practices of retroactive legislation. A distinction must be drawn between tax legislation which is, by its very nature, subject to ongoing modification and a
February 12, 1990

situation such as represented by Bill C-26 with a termination of a longstanding subsidy program has caused serious economic dislocation for the affected regions and industries in Saint John and Halifax.
Second, this bill was on the Order Paper for seven months before it was brought before this House and there has been serious economic upheaval created in the maritimes by a de facto decision of a department of this government. This was done not because of any instructions, order or decision made in this House. If Your Honour so finds that there is a prima facie case, I would be pleased to make the appropriate motion.

speakeroldname: Hon. Shirley Martin (for the Minister of Transport) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-26, an act to amend the Railway Act (grain and flour subsidies), be read a second time and referred to a legislative committee.
She said: Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to open the debate on second reading of Bill C-26, an act to amend the Railway Act. This government is committed to building a strong economy, an economy encouraged by incentive and opportunity, an economy which is competitive with the world's trading nations.
In order to fully achieve this goal we must create a solid base which will allow our economy to flourish in coming years. Measures which seek to control the deficit and reduce the national debt are an essential element of this foundation for the future. Equally, measures which seek to establish a sound fiscal framework to sustain a continued economic development are also essential to our purpose.
These objectives are reflected in this government's commitment to a sound transportation policy. Transportation is and always will be at the heart of our nation's economy. That is why we have undertaken to provide Canadians with a safe, efficient and effective transportation system. This commitment is the core around which our policy of economic regulatory reform was built.
With the advent of the free trade policy and the role played by transportation in our economic development, it is becoming increasingly vital as we enter this new decade and in the next centuiy. A cost effective transportation system is essential if Canada is to preserve and enhance its position in world trade. Therefore, the bill now before this House seeks to eliminate a subsidy which has outlived its original purpose and has become a burden on the public purse.

February 12, 1990
Government Orders
By way of background, Bill C-26 deals with a transportation subsidy which is commonly known as the at and east subsidy. This rather odd name evolved from an attempt to counterbalance American freight rates which would encourage the movement of western Canadian grain between Buffalo, New York, and the port of New York City during the winter freeze up on the Great Lakes; in other words, movements at and east of Buffalo. The subsidy which was introduced in an effort to counter this U.S. initiative and to keep our winter grain movements on Canadian soil quickly became known as the at and east subsidy.
The subsidy gave shipping rail rates to eastern ports which were frozen at the 1960 rate for grain and the 1966 rate for flour. The government then paid the railways an amount equal to the difference between the frozen rates and the actual cost of the movement. The level of the subsidy was independently determined by the National Transportation Agency.
The amounts of grain which move under the at and east subsidy represent less than 3 per cent of our total grain exports in a normal year. Various impact studies have been done on this subsidy in the past 15 years. They have all acknowledged that the at and east subsidy no longer serves the purpose for which it was originally intended. Canadian ports and railways can now compete effectively with their American counterparts for eastern exports of grain and flour.
Canadian taxpayers cannot afford to pay subsidies based on a 1960 policy which is no longer required. Savings are expected to be about $20 million in the first year and some $35 to $40 million annually thereafter. The subsidy was terminated on July 15, 1989.
However, the legislation stipulates that all inventories of grain and flour which were held by the railways on that date would be delivered at the subsidized rate, provided they reach the eastern port for export on or before January 31, 1990. This sixth-month period allowed for a smooth transition thereby minimizing the impact on the users.
Pre-confederation Canada had to struggle constantly to meet its transportation challenges. This rugged land of vast spaces needed unifying bonds. Our early needs for unification were met through the realization of Sir John A. Macdonald's grand dream of a transcontinental railway. The openings of the St. Lawrence Seaway and
the Trans-Canada Highway in 1959 and 1962 had enormous positive impacts on economic development and transportation. With new and ever growing technology, our expanding airwaves and communication have reduced the size of this country, and we are all now truly neighbours in this great nation.
Transportation must continue to play its vital role as we enter this new decade and the next century. In looking forward I see a transportation system with at least four essential elements: first and foremost, it will be safe; second, it will be efficient and effective, that is, it will make the best use of each mode of transportation, be it air, rail, marine, car, truck or bus; third, it will be responsive, that is, it will meet the needs of shippers and travellers; fourth, it will be innovative, both in the use of technology and in the services it offers.
The bill currently before us is one step in that direction. It will stimulate creativity and innovation. It will allow the industry to take advantage of unanticipated sales opportunities, no longer constraining potential cost savings.
Direct federal government expenditures associated with the grain transportation are very large. It must be remembered that the Canadian grain industry faces severe competition in world markets. A cost effective transportation system is essential, if Canada is to preserve its position in the world of grain trade. We must face the realities of our economy and our transportation system. Bill C-26 does just that. Therefore, I invite all members to give this legislation their full support.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to this bill today as a member of Parliament, as one who has spent a lifetime in the agricultural industry, and as one who recognizes the benefits that came from this particular bill, not just to farmers in Ontario but farmers all across western Canada.
It shocks me that the government would be withdrawing this at and east legislation at a time when the minister's own figures point out that for the coming year farm income will drop in Canada by 39 per cent: 101 per cent in the province of Saskatchewan and 87 per cent in Manitoba. Literally thousands of farmers across this nation are losing their farms, partly because of the callous disregard for their industry by this government and partly because of the cut-backs in funding. The

cut-back for the coming year will see the income drop by $2.6 billion, a drop of 64 per cent. We see these cut-backs taking place at a time when our neighbours to the south with whom we have that free trade agreement are gearing up to increase their export enhancement program for next year. This year the export enhancement program will see at least $566 million pumped into their export programs.
When the minister said that they are building a better, stronger economy, an economy that is competitive, I must ask: how do we compete with the subsidies of other countries when we are cutting ours out? Who is bearing the burden? The farmers are bearing this burden on their shoulders. It is coming to the point when they can no longer carry that burden and carry the rest of society.
They say that it is to reduce the deficit. The increase in taxes in the last budget on alcoholic products and tobacco was $475 million. The moneys spent on the at and east are a drop in the bucket compared to that.
We hear that free trade has made it vital to develop a cost effective transportation system. I would like to know how we can move the grain through the Seaway system with the winters we have in Canada, whereas the Mississippi waterway largely stays open for most of its length during the year. It seems very strange indeed that while we are cutting back on subsidies here in Canada, our neighbours to the south with whom we are competing for world markets are increasing theirs.
The at and east legislation was brought in, in the 1960s, not just to help the western farmers or the Ontario farmers. It was brought in for a very specific reason based on the fact that we needed a place to consolidate our grain shipments for export. We had flour mills in Atlantic Canada that needed a steady supply of grain over the winter months. Consequently the grains eligible for at and east rates included wheat, wheat flour, oats, barley, rye, corn, buckwheat and soybeans. For bulk grains, the subsidy applied for rail shipment from Georgian Bay in Ontario. This is where I as a farmer was able to make use of that program through our marketing boards that stored the grain in those Bayport elevators for shipment later on during freeze up to the Atlantic
Government Orders
coast to supply those flour mills and those ports by rail, for export.
Last winter the Canadian Wheat Board moved only 202,730 tonnes of prairie grain under the at and east rates, with 25,192 tonnes going to Quebec City and the rest to the Atlantic ports in Halifax and Saint John. On average, the rail shipments by the Canadian Wheat Board have been more like 400,000 to 500,000 tonnes per year.
What we are doing here is withdrawing the subsidy. Those markets in Atlantic Canada will now be available for imported grain out of the Texas gulf coast or other countries. Again Canadian producers will be deprived of another market. It is also interesting to note that local feed grains produced in Atlantic Canada only account for 20 per cent of Nova Scotia's requirements, 35 to 40 per cent of New Brunswick's requirements, and 80 per cent of Prince Edward Island's requirements.
That is going to cast an additional burden on the livestock and poultry producers of Atlantic Canada, as well as put a burden on and take a grain market away from farmers in the west.
I look at the amount of the United States grain that has been sold under the export enhancement program with subsidies that range from $6.48 a tonne back in September 21, to the most recent sale where they sold almost half a million tonnes of wheat to Russia with subsidies of $20.50 a tonne. I would ask the government to reconsider what it is doing by way of throwing these markets open to the vultures of the market-place and depriving them of Canadian grown grain of higher quality that can fill those markets.
In the budget that was leaked last April there was a total of $399 million listed that would not be available to the farmers of Canada. For example, a $200 million cut in crop insurance, $60 million for the at and east legislation before us today, rail branch line rehabilitation of $48 million, the grain and crop advance payments of $54 million, dairy exports of $12 million, commodity based loans at the Farm Credit Corporation of $15 million, and the Canadian Dairy Commission of $12 million.
When I see programs like that being discontinued, apparently under the guise of cutting back the deficit, I wonder how much of this was cut back in order to conform to the free trade agreement. Then I read where the Secretary of Agriculture of the United States told

Government Orders
the United States Senate last April 19, that he intended to write agricultural policies not only for the United States but also for the European Common Market, Canada, Argentina, Brazil, Australia and so on.
I have to wonder if this legislation is some of his handiwork and if he has convinced the government to cut back on these and leave our producers out hanging in the breeze to wither and die when their subsidies are cut off. These subsidies have enabled them to compete very effectively over the years with the large geographical expanse that we have in this nation, to make their products available at the seaports on either side, east or west, and to provide jobs to the Canadian people.
In terms of the loss of jobs, according to the report of the Canadian Transport Commission on the at and east the following direct job benefits to the program were identified: 320 jobs connected with transport, 295 jobs in milling in western Canada, 75 jobs in the Georgian Bay ports, 85 jobs in Halifax and Saint John, and milling in central Canada was 402 jobs. Almost 1,200 jobs are connected to this piece of legislation.
The downturn in the economy in Atlantic Canada, and the disastrous impact resulting from the closure of the fish plants, is an equally hard blow to those people in Atlantic Canada. This program that served them so well should be continued and enhanced to make our milling companies, flour mills and ports competitive with those of our neighbours to the south.
The benefit of utilizing the at and east route for the Ontario wheat producers, for example, is very clear. It enables them to average export sales over the winter months. They have a system of pool pricing whereby they are able to do this, but they are providing importing countries with a continuous supply of grain, while yielding the producers the best average return.
The importing countries that are mentioned are buying this high quality wheat from Canada, the pasta wheat, and the at and east legislation allows the Wheat Board to keep a portion of the total volume of Ontario export grain temporarily off the market and spread those sales throughout the year to act as a hedge against a drop in price.
However this government does not think that way. It is quite content to sell it to the very large multinational grain companies and let them have control of it at harvest time and then reap the benefits of any price increases. Typically, under this system that we have at the present time, if the price is not acceptable to the Wheat Board it will choose to stay off the market and eventually move the grain by at and east, if necessary, when the price is more favourable, and since this route is subsidized, the Ontario wheat producers can use it with little financial penalty.
They say that in due consideration of the economics associated with the at and east program as applied to the total marketing system, the Ontario Wheat Board considers the program to be invaluable to its operation and to the interests of all facets of the industry. For the amount of dollars expended on the subsidy program it may be the best and least expensive insurance plan available to the eastern marketing system. That not only includes the Wheat Board. It also includes the elevators, the flour mills and the ports that I mentioned earlier.
Already the impact of this is showing up in the Bayport elevators in Georgian Bay. One of them is slated for demolition this year because of the loss of this legislation. This is another blow to the economy of those ports. I hesitate to say: "Forgive them Lord for they know not what they do".
Removal of the program would also reduce the income of the grain producers of Ontario in the amount of $3.60 a tonne, according to a Department of Agriculture working paper. They went on to make the statement that combined with the lack of transportation facilities and inadequate storage capacity the cost increase would have been more adversely affected across the country.
This attack on the maritimes too cannot be condoned. It may result in even less rail service, for if grain is no longer shipped by rail by the Canadian Wheat Board and the Ontario Wheat Growers Marketing Board the viability of several lines is put in question.
In 1988, according to the National Transportation Agency, 722,000 tonnes of export grain and 222,322 tonnes of export flour moved under the at and east rate structure. Atlantic ports represent 90 per cent of the total tonnage. If the program terminated and the elevators remained operational, $14 million in economic activity will be lost and the loss of feed costs would be
February 12, 1990

$222,000. Local milling producers would be faced with a loss of their only market should the flour mill in Halifax be unable to continue. It would result in a higher procurement costs for the feed industry and higher feed prices.
The maritimes are dealing with abandonment of approximately 50 per cent of the rail network in the region. Any loss of traffic which will affect the viability of the remaining lines is viewed as a very serious matter.
Canadian flour exports will be practically non-existent without the subsidy. This is a statement made by the Canadian Transport Commission. In the case of the flour milling industry it is likely that the size and scope of this sector will be greatly reduced. The export market might well disappear unless the government introduces some sort of assistance. Fred Hanson, flour co-ordinator of the Canadian National Millers Association, said that Halifax will lose business to Montreal and other western Canadian ports. I think the ports of Halifax and Saint John will be hard pressed to remain competitive.
The government looks upon the at and east as a subsidy. We should look at it rather as a positive effect on exports, yet here we are removing it. As I mentioned earlier, the export enhancement program in the United States is being maintained and increased. Indeed the government's and the minister's own Green Paper laments the lack of exports from Canada of highly processed agri-food products, noting that only 2 per cent of our total food exports are processed. Yet one hand does not know what the other hand is doing, because they are taking away this subsidy and then complaining about the fact that we do not have enough processing in Canada.
Similar to the advance payments for crops, The Budget Papers only identify partially the purpose of the program to rationalize the removal of the interest-free payments. This itself put the farmers of Canada under a further burden, and yet piece by piece we have seen the support systems of Canadian agriculture taken away at a time when we have to be competitive in world markets. We are playing the Boy Scouts while all the other countries are getting behind their producers and assisting them to be competitive, whether it is through subsidies or export enhancement programs that we see here in North
Government Orders
America or some of the subsidies of the European Common Market.
This program was brought in, in 1966, by the the hon. John Pickersgill. He stated that according to the Board of Transport Commissioners these rates were already unremunerative. We decided to keep those rates at the present level and pay compensation for doing so because we felt there was an obligation in the east with regard to the Crow's Nest Pass rate. The purpose was to ensure that we would have rates that would provide some inducement and incentive to shippers to use the facilities of the Atlantic ports.
Even 24 years ago the administration at that time realized full well that we had to have some assistance to those Atlantic ports to ensure a flow of product to the east that provided jobs and opportunities and the continuity of product to keep those mills running over the winter months.
Cancelling this program will only reduce the federal deficit by approximately $40 million. It cannot be said that cancelling a program contributes in a meaningful way to reducing the deficit. I referred to this a moment ago, that it is piecemeal at the very least.
The current tax paid by the agricultural industry is far greater than the total expenditure of the agriculture budget. Agriculture not only pays its way, but it contributes to the fiscal budget in a very positive way and contributes to the balance of trade. We have seen our trade surplus plummet this last fall. I would have to suggest that with the withdrawal of the at and east subsidy it is going to plummet even further.
The government talks about an economy that is competitive. Our producers are competitive here in Canada. We are among the best in the world, the most competitive in terms of productivity.
For example, milk production per cow has gone up 70 per cent in Canada since 1971. During the same period in the United States it rose by only 46 per cent. If we want to judge efficiency by price we look at poultry. We see that while the real farm gate price of poultry has dropped by 30 per cent since the 1970s, the retail price has just dropped by 10 per cent over the same period. Who is the most efficient? Is it the farmers or the food processing industry?

February 12, 1990
Government Orders
In terms of the farm gate chicken price in 1982, it represented 48 per cent of the final cost to the consumer. Now it accounts for only 38 per cent of the cost. Clearly these figures demonstrate that orderly marketing is efficient and contributes to the financial well-being of the Canadian agricultural industry.
Part of the efficiency that we saw here is through the orderly marketing and the ability to move products to market over the full 12 months of the year. That is why this legislation was put in place in the 1966 era.
It served us well and we certainly saw the advantages of it, not just for Ontario or Atlantic Canada.
We saw it for the Canadian Wheat Board. We saw it for the creation of jobs on the prairies. When I consider that it is going to cut this back at a period when our agricultural industry in the prairies perhaps is in a more difficult position that it was in the 1930s, it is unconscionable that we should have cut-backs of this magnitude to a program that has served us so well.
I call on the government at this point to withdraw this legislation and reconsider what it is doing. It has been seven months since the budget and this is the first day that this has been introduced into this House. It has caused pandemonium not only in the transportation industry but in the Canadian and Ontario Wheat Boards which are trying to sell their products not knowing whether or not it applied. It is a piece of legislation that was made retroactive and was followed by a drop in price. It was compounded by another drop in price some six or seven months later when the United States made that huge sale of grain to Russia that was subsidized to the tune of $20.50 a tonne or 56 cents per bushel.
I have to question the wisdom of this move at a time of severe financial difficulty across this country in the rural areas. There are whole communities in western Canada, particularly in Saskatchewan, where businesses are closing because they depend on the agriculture industry. They are the main businesses in those towns and as the agriculture industry faces hardships, those businesses are forced to close as well.
We should be going in the opposite direction. If we are going to compete with our neighbours to the south, the government has an obligation to put the money forward
to assist the farmers to move that grain to market. It should not be left to the primary producers to carry this burden. It is an obligation of the government to assist them. It is an obligation of society because a lot of this product is moving into export, and every export dollar earned contributes to our Canadian economy.
In conclusion, I would ask that the government reconsider this legislation. It should reinstate this program and enhance it to a level that would make us competitive with Americans programs which they are utilizing and are using to steal our markets.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: It is my duty, pursuant to Standing Order 38, to inform the House that the questions to be raised tonight at the time of adjournment are as follows: the hon. member for Vancouver East, Immigration; the hon. member for Kingston and the Islands, Canada Elections Act; the hon. member for Halifax, Violence Against Women.

The at
and east program has been in existence for almost a quarter of a century and in fact has been an important element of the maritime economy. Bill C-26, which will remove the program, means a potential loss of over $27 million to the maritimes and over 250 direct jobs to the economies, primarily of Saint John and Halifax. Not only is it tragic that this program is being removed formally but the way in which the government has handled Bill C-26 reveals a more fundamental principle. The way in which this government has handled the bill displays an arrogance, a conceit and a self-centredness of the PC Party and this government.
Through this bill they have displayed a disrespect for this institution of Parliament. That is simply by the fact that they have implemented this bill, de facto, before the bill has actually been debated in this House. The legislation for at and east is found in the Railway Act. It is a program that encourages export shippers of grain and flour to use eastern ports.
This is a program that affects grain and flour somewhat differently. With respect to grain, the program is applicable to export grain that is shipped by rail from points at lake ports on Georgian Bay, Lake Huron, Lake Ontario and the upper St. Lawrence as far as Prescott and if the rail destination is any port on the St. Lawrence from Montreal east as well as the ports of Saint John and Halifax. With respect to flour the program is applicable if
February 12, 1990

flour is shipped by rail for export from Thunder Bay east, again to the same ports.
This program has evolved so that shippers of grain are charged rates that were in effect in 1960 while flour shippers pay the rate that was in effect in 1966. The difference between those rates and the compensatory rates are paid to the railways by the government.
The hon. minister indicated that the reason for enacting this program was that initially there had been worry about competition from the United States. I can point out to the minister that that is only part of the case. In fact, the Hon. G. W. Pickersgill who was then the Minister of Transport stated when the legislation was under consideration back in the 1960s that it also meant: "To ensure that we will have rates which will provide some inducement and incentive to shippers to use the facilities of Atlantic ports."
In other words, in addition to ensuring that eastern Canadian ports could compete with U.S. ports the at and east rates were also intended to enable the ports of Halifax and Saint John to compete with Montreal and other St. Lawrence River ports. This had the effect of creating and maintaining jobs primarily in the Maritimes. In other words, it was a good regional program.
There is another aspect with respect to the American angle, that is the program offset a geographic advantage that the U.S. has because of shorter hauling distances to ports. With the removal of the at and east, this advantage is gone. There is a real irony here. This government talks so much about creating a level playing field that the term is rapidly becoming a cliche. Yet the government and the PC party seem to have completely forgotten about the level playing field concept with respect to this bill and with respect to regional programs throughout the country.
It may well be that the at and east needs some revision and should be looked at, but by simply cancelling the program the government has forsaken the notion of a level playing field in the maritimes. There seems to have been somewhat of a change of attitude by the government in that it has talked before about creating level playing fields in order to create equality and fairness for Canadians. It is very clear by this and many other examples that this government has no intention of
Government Orders
creating equity and fairness or level playing fields for average Canadians at all.
The government's politics are very transparent. It is purely and simply promoting a 19th century laissez-faire economy-today it is called neo-conservatism-which is simply a philosophy that will allow the rich to stay rich and in fact become richer by stealing more of this country's wealth.
It is a philosophy that benefits the few at the expense of the majority. It is a philosophy that did not work in the 1800s and a philosophy that does not work today in spite of the fancy packaging that this government employs.
The at and east program has become an important part of the diversification of the maritime economy. Any region of the country that depends on one industry is in a very tenuous situation should that industry fail. Although the fishing industry is not the only industry in the maritimes, it has played a vital role in a viable maritime economy.
We all know that industry is now in a very bad way and although the Prime Minister assures us that there is no crisis in the maritimes, I would suggest to the Prime Minister and to the minister that they are trying to ensure that if in fact the maritimes are not quite over the edge, yet they will provide that little extra push with the passage of this bill.
There is a need to encourage and promote diversification in all regions of this country. That has been a fundamental plank of virtually every federal government since Confederation up until the present one. The Prime Minister and the members of his cabinet today have abandoned this fundamental principle, this basic building block to our nation's economy.
I am from Saskatchewan where we have witnessed and felt the cold, harsh reality of PC politics. We in the west have much in common with folks in the maritimes. In our rural communities we have seen our economic base undermined. We have seen our post offices disappearing. We have seen VIA Rail abruptly removed. We have seen services removed for seniors in communities where they can no longer remain, where they have lived all their lives, as in the maritimes. We have seen unemployment figures rise. We have seen people leaving our region of the country and we have seen the growth of food banks and record numbers of people living below the poverty line. In fact, in Saskatchewan now there are more people
