living below the poverty line than anywhere in Canada, except for Newfoundland, and that is with two Tory governments, federal and provincial.
At the same time, we have been forced to listen to a finance minister who tells us that we have had good economic growth for the last few years but now we have to tighten our belts. I would like to tighten something as well. It would not be a belt, it would be a political noose around the political neck of the government. However, I think the government is doing a very good job of tightening its own noose these days.
The minister may want to tighten our belts, but for the maritimes the government is simply shutting the door with this bill. Without a doubt, this bill hits the maritimes very hard. The Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission has completed several studies into the impact of the at and east.
With all due respect, contrary to the minister's statement that all reports that had come out indicated it was time to remove the at and east, that is not true. The Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission has in fact issued a number of reports. It has concluded that the at and east has had a significant impact on the ports of Halifax and Saint John.
I would point out to the minister that in 1988 some 338,000 tonnes of export grain and 183,000 tonnes of export flour moved through the port of Halifax. Tonnage for Saint John in 1988 was approximately 246,000 tonnes of export grain and 1,200 tonnes of export flour. This represents approximately 90 per cent of the total tonnage that was moved out of the at and east program in 1988.
It is a maritime program. These figures represent almost all the grain handled at the Saint John elevator and approximately 60 per cent of the volume handled at the elevator at Halifax. Now that the program has been implemented, despite not being passed by Parliament, the elevator at Saint John is now going to be closing because it cannot receive grain by water. It can only receive grain by rail, and nobody is shipping grain by rail to Saint John now that the program is gone. So it is costing jobs.
The loss of this program is going to affect more than grain elevators. Port employment will be affected, railway employment will be affected and there will be negative effects on flour millers, particularly Dover Mills in Halifax. I would like to quote from a report that the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission submitted in September 1989. Obviously the minister has not seen it.
In the report it is stated that an analysis by the commission of the regional impact of the program showed that approximately $14.4 million in economic activity will be lost to the region due to the termination of the subsidy. However, should both grain elevators in the region at Halifax and Saint John be unable to continue operations, the negative impact would amount to approximately $27.6 million. These amounts do not include any economic activity generated by the program which occurred outside the Atlantic region such as railway employment, inland elevators, lake vessels, et cetera. It has affected ports in the Ontario region as well.
It goes on to state in the second paragraph on page 3 of this report that the importance of maintaining the Halifax grain elevator as a viable operation is of critical economic importance to the entire Atlantic region. As well as the activity generated by the movement of export grain to the facility, the elevator also plays a vital role in the storage and handling of domestic feed grain and milling wheat.
Local pork, poultry and egg industries and to a lesser extent the beef industries would be seriously affected should the Halifax elevator be unable to remain in operation.
In addition, the Halifax elevator is utilized as the only means of storage for milling wheat by the only Atlantic region flour mill, Dover Flour Mills. If the elevator should close in Halifax, Dover Flour Mills will probably close as well. If the minister does not have all three reports, I will be glad to provide them to her because they are very interesting reading. They provide a good insight into the importance of this program to the maritimes.
The fact that 250 direct jobs will be lost and $27 million will be lost is only one part of it. The secondary impact is going to be just as devastating. I was in the maritimes last fall and had occasion to speak with some farmers in Prince Edward Island. Prince Edward Island has a lot of
February 12, 1990

family farms. There are good family operations which grow potatoes and hay or raise hogs.
These people indicated to me that they rely on western grains because, although they grow about 80 per cent of the feed grains that they use on the island, they still need the high quality grains which come from the west.
I talked the President of Dover Flour Mills a number of times. He indicated that business has dropped some 20 per cent. In fact, Dover has lost all the competitive markets in the world in the face of the loss of this subsidy and because of the high dollar. Dover Flour Mills is simply left with CIDA projects. Canada is reducing subsidies at the same time that the U.S. is putting on subsidies.
According to the government, the free trade agreement was going to be of benefit to Canada because it would open up agricultural markets for Canadians. Although Americans have been talking of no subsidies in public, certainly officials have been telling me in private-and I am sure the government-that subsidies will remain high and perhaps get even higher.
We have seen the attack that the U.S. has levelled against Canadian agriculture. It used GATT to obtain entrance for its dairy products into Canada. It countervailed and is using harassing tactics to keep Canadians hogs and pork out of the U.S. It is threatening an attack on the use of the Western Grain Transportation Act, that is if this government does not remove it first.
What have we done in response? What did Canada do when George Bush put forward a budget calling for some $900 million for export grain subsidies and attacked our conventional markets? The U.S.S.R. has indicated it is going to buy some 12 million tonnes of grain this year and the United States has announced that it will subsidize up to three million tonnes which go to the U.S.S.R. That is a direct effect on Canada's market. What has this government done? Nothing. The government is monitoring the situation.
What is the possible logic behind this? There is no logic, if you believe in fair opportunities for Canadians in all regions of the country. There is no logic, if you believe in maintaining and promoting viable communities with viable industries in all areas of Canada. In fact,
Government Orders
the direction this government is taking is purely and simply counterproductive to a viable, healthy economy.
It is a joke that this is supposed to be a government and a party which has the answers to the economic problems of this country. The government's answers may be beneficial for the Conrad Blacks of the world in assisting them to devour more and more of this country's wealth, but they certainly do nothing for the average Canadian.
In fact, I find it insulting and I am sure many Canadians find it insulting when the finance minister says that we have just come through good times. I think most Canadians will agree that the success of a nation is not measured by how many millionaires we have, how many domed stadiums we possess or how many Canadians can afford to travel to exotic places.
Rather, I believe that most Canadians would measure this country's success by how few homeless we have, how few people we have living below the poverty line and how few people need to use food banks. That is how success ought to be measured. In using this measurement for this government, it is quite clear that the government has failed and it has failed very badly, not for the Conrad Blacks but for average Canadians.
Yet this government is not reluctant to remove some $27 million annually and some 250 direct jobs from the maritimes. The indirect impact, as discussed earlier, will have a much broader impact to all comers of the maritimes. In addition, I have been advised that CP Rail line which goes to Saint John may no longer be viable now that the Saint John elevator is closed and the tonnage will no longer be coming.
Not only will the maritimes suffer, but this bill will have a ripple effect right across the country. Port McNicoll, Ontario, has been shut. In talking with the Canadian Wheat Board the other day they indicated that they used to send some 300,000 tonnes of grain every year through the port of Halifax alone. Now that has been reduced to something like 100,000 tonnes a year, and it may disappear altogether. They have a concern because if the port of Halifax closes-now that the port of Saint John has closed-there will be no ice free ports on the eastern seaboard in Canada. There will be none.

February 12, 1990
Government Orders
The Canadian Wheat Board has indicated that some purchasers of grain do not want to come into Montreal, even though it is kept open during the year, because of the ice. In fact, Cuba is a good example. Presently Cuba is buying some grain from Canada and is using Halifax port to pick up that grain.
The Canadian Wheat Board has indicated to me that all things being equal, if the Halifax port is no longer there Cuba may go somewhere else. We will be losing grain sales which we can ill afford to lose, which we are losing at a high number right now and as a result of which we are threatened in our traditional markets. We are going to shoot ourselves in the foot by closing these two ports.
The people in the maritimes have long appreciated this program. They have also been concerned about the cost of the program and ensuring that the federal government was receiving its money's worth. In fact, in 1985, as I indicated earlier, the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission presented two briefs to this government. It outlined an alternative to the existing program.
Contrary to what the minister says, there have been briefs presented that do not want the program removed. They outline an alternative to the existing program. They did not propose to cancel the program but proposed changes to the program that would cut the cost of the program in half.
They volunteered this in 1985 when the program was costing between $34 million and $40 million. They presented a proposal that would save the government $20 million a year. The government ignored it. There were changes that they said would cut the program in half without eliminating any aspect of the program while maintaining a vital maritime economy. What do you suppose was the government's response to this well thought out proposal? What do you suppose the government said to the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission?
I and my fellow colleagues have been reminded numerous times by various ministers of this government's commitment to consultation. I and my colleagues have been told in sometimes not very flattering terms that when we have accused the government of not only not consulting with Canadians but not paying attention to Canadians, this government does consult. They point
out that this government is one that pays attention to Canadians' needs, that it defines and develops programs for the benefit of all Canadians. Therefore, I would assume that it would at least take this proposal seriously.
The Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission is not a fly-by-night group. It is a longstanding, very well respected organization representing a cross section of Atlantic Canada. It presented not just one brief in 1985, but two well documented, well thought out briefs in which it outlined how the government could change the at and east program and save $20 million a year.
What sort of response did it get from this considerate government? It could be summed up in one sentence from the third report that it submitted last September. The APTC, the commission, has never received a response to the proposals from the federal government. It never received a response, not even a peep, not so much as a whisper.
It is not that the government read the report and called representatives in to explain the proposal in detail, that it asked them to make changes, or that it acknowledged that it received the report and would be considering it. They never received a response, not even a thank you letter.
The minister has indicated that there has been no proposal that the At and East program remain. By not repsonding to these well thought out presentations, the government is displaying its arrogance. It is displaying the fact that it has lost touch with the real people of this country. In short, this government is displaying the fact that it simply does not give a damn for anyone or any group that does not agree with this government. It does not matter if you are a potato farmer in P.E.I., it does not matter if you are a lawyer in Halifax or if you are the president of the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission.
Not only is this government arrogant to the people of Canada, it has been disrespectful to Parliament, disrespectful because it has already enacted Bill C-26 without the approval of Parliament. That is nothing new, it has already invoked closure 11 times, more times than any other government in the history of this country.
By taking this most unfortunate step the government has almost guaranteed that there would be no changes whatsoever to this bill at any stage. The reason is very
February 12, 1990

clear that if Parliament should decide not to enact this bill or to enact another bill that would maintain the program, the government may well find that it is liable to the tune of millions of dollars for the way that people have been responding given the de facto actions of the Department of Transport.
On May 4, 1989, Transport Canada officials held a meeting with shippers and the railways to advise them that the at and east program rates would terminate effective July 15, 1989, and that on all contracts commencing on July 16 they were to charge compensatory rates.
Parliament has not passed any such legislation. In fact if any interested parties should decide to challenge this decision, I am quite sure now that they would be successful and could force the government to actually follow the law. Fortunately for this government no challenge has come forward.
If it should ever come to pass that Parliament should enact the law that is different than what is proposed in Bill C-26, then we may find that an at and east program still exists. If that should come to pass and certain businesses take this government at its word-which is a mistake-and found that they had relied on false assumptions and as a result have suffered significant losses, I suggest that the Department of Transport would find itself in a severe legal position.
As such the government is, to say the least, going to be extremely reluctant to amend any aspect of this bill. The government will argue that there is a retroactive clause and that Bill C-26 can pass validly. It is not uncommon to have retroactive legislation. These, however, are usual with respect to tax matters which are often made retroactive to budget night in order to prevent avoidance by taxpayers during the period between the budget and the date of the enactment of the law.
It is held, however, that this power to enact retroactive laws must be exercised with appropriate restraint. It is unfortunate that this government is acting with reckless abandon. I would suggest that a distinction can be made between the tax legislation which is by its nature subject to ongoing modification and a situation such as that represented by this bill before the House today. Termination of a longstanding subsidy program is having a

serious economic dislocation for the affected areas, namely Saint John and Halifax.
As well, this government has been further inconsiderate of Parliament as an institution by not bringing this matter before Parliament before now. It has been eight months since Bill C-26 was given first reading and seven months since it was enforced de facto.
I believe this government has displayed a callous disregard for Parliament. As a result of this action the work of the legislative committee will be very difficult. It could well be that once the alternatives suggested by the commission are looked at and given serious attention, which they obviously have not been given until now, there may well be alternatives forthcoming to this present bill. If the government agrees to these changes it will be difficult to enact them because of the action it has taken to date.
In conclusion, this is a bill that displays the government's lack of commitment for regional development. If the government did consult, if it was considerate, it would be having serious discussions with these groups. It would be having discussions with the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission.
There are other groups which it should have consulted in considering its program. There is Dover Flour Mill in Halifax, the port of Saint John, the city of Saint John, the Canadian Feed Industry Association which is going to be affected by this bill, the Halifax grain elevator, the Halifax Port Commission, the Nova Scotia Grains Commission, the Nova Scotia Grain Marketing Board, the Nova Scotia Federation of Agriculture, and the Maritime Farmers Council. They are all very concerned about the loss of this program because it is very likely going to mean the loss of the elevators at Halifax and Saint John.
As the Canadian Wheat Board indicated, the elevator at Halifax, which can receive grain by water, will have difficulty bringing out a shipload of grain because it cannot buy a full allotment at one time. At Halifax the elevator has been buying feed grain and the Canadian Wheat Board has been topping this up in order to get a full shipment out. If the Canadian Wheat Board should decide not to send grain to Halifax that will be the end of the Halifax elevator, it will be finished.

Government Orders
The Dover Flour Mill uses the Halifax elevator as a storage facility for the grain used for its flour. If the elevator closes, the Dover Flour Mill will be unable to take over the Halifax elevator because it would not be economically viable, and mill will close. The Dover Flour Mill is the only flour mill that exists in Atlantic Canada because of this program. It has now been placed in jeopardy.
As well, the ripple effect through the whole agricultural community in the maritimes is devastating, not to mention the dock workers who are employed for the movement of flour, but also the rail crews that are now being eliminated. There are 250 direct jobs and numerous indirect jobs which will be lost.
This bill will rob the maritimes of at least $27 million and 250 jobs directly, not mention the spin-off affect. It is tragic, that this government did not take the time to consult with the people of the maritimes. It is tragic that it did not consider the proposal of the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission five years ago. In 1985 it presented an alternative that would save the government $20 million a year, which would have amounted to a $100 million now. It is unfortunate that this government did not consider that report some five years ago.
I call upon the government to stop its actions, to announce that the at and east program will continue and to take a serious look at the commission's reports. It put together not one but three reports. It called for this government to make changes. It volunteered changes to the at and east payments. The commission said that changes should be happening and suggested how it should be done.
This bill makes it very clear that the government has no regard for the average people of this country or the constitution of Parliament. It is a government that has lost touch with the people. There is a good news and a bad news aspect to this whole thing. The goods news is that the people of Canada realize that this is the kind of attitude this government has taken and they are going to toss this government out on its ear. The bad news is that we have to wait two and a half years. The good news is that tonight in the riding of Chambly we are going to start that process by electing our first New Democratic
member of Parliament in the history of the province of Quebec.
I call on this government to reconsider its bill. I call on this government to look at the commission's report. I call on this government to take seriously the issues that are of concern to the people of the maritimes, such as economics. I call on this government to look seriously at this bill and to make some real changes to the at and east program so that we can maintain a viable economic situation, so that we can maintain the viable infrastructure that has existed for 25 years in the maritimes.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Under Standing Order 74 the first three speakers had 40 minutes for debate. There were no questions or comments. We are now entering the period when there will be 20 minute speeches with ten minutes for questions and comments. The hon. member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to rise and comment on Bill C-26, the bill which gives effect to the cancellation of the at and east program announced in the April 27, 1989 budget.
May I echo, as an Atlantic Canadian, the words of those who have spoken before me, at least the two members who come from the opposition side of the House, that indeed the cancellation of this program is yet another blow at the fragile economy of Atlantic Canada. It is a blow that is being delivered at a time when our people and our economy lay shattered from one bad news scenario after another.
We had massive route abandonment on the railways in Atlantic Canada. The loss of the at and east contributes even further to the lack of viability of the railways in Atlantic Canada. Our fishery has been under incredible, heretofore unimagined assault. Individuals, fishing communities and, indeed, the economy indirectly all the way back to the major suppliers at the major centres are reeling under that blow.
We have had a 39 per cent reduction over the last five years of regional development spending in Atlantic Canada, an abandonment of the principle of combating regional disparity. In the agricultural sector, which is perhaps in some respects most fragile in all of Canada in the Atlantic region, we have had the cancellation, completely without consultation, completely without discussing the impact with anybody, of the at and east
February 12, 1990

program, a program that has been around for approximately 25 years.
A program, yes, with faults, but one that has been veiy successful in contributing to the orderly marketing and export of grains in the region. Perhaps most frustrating is not that this program was cancelled completely without consultation with anybody in Atlantic Canada, or with anybody in the agricultural community across this country, because it impacts very directly on the farmers of Ontario and western Canada, but the fact that, although notice was given last April 27 of the cancellation of this program, it is only today, February 12, 1990, that the legislation giving effect to that cancellation is before the House.
Most Canadians who are not familiar with the at and east are saying, "Well, at least you had all that notice to get ready for the impact of the loss of that subsidy. At least you had time to contemplate it, time to make your case and time to prepare for the bill going to a legislative committee of Parliament, the Standing Committee of Transport, time for the people of Atlantic Canada to lobby their MPs and ministers of the Crown, time for Atlantic provincial governments to make their case and to come to Ottawa and ensure that their voices were heard". That is what the average Canadian watching these proceedings believes to be the case.
The reality is that Parliament is only today, for the first time, debating the ramifications of this bill and the loss of this program. The fact is that the cuts have already been put in place by the railways, that the impact of the loss of the at and east has been factored into the pricing arrangements of the railways for the last number of months. It is a fait accomplis. It has happened.
This Parliament is not even a rubber stamp under this government's administration. This Parliament has become a joke. It is irrelevant. Is it any wonder that people are screaming for a different kind of system, a different kind of Parliament, a Senate where every province is equal, a Senate that has the capability, when rights have been crushed, to veto the actions of the elected Parliament in a substantial and meaningful way.
This system has made a mockery of the notion that the people of Atlantic Canada have democratic rights. We had an announcement in April of 1989, we had immedi-
Govemment Orders
ate implementation, and seven or eight months later we are asked to consider it in Parliament. This Parliament, with its stained glass windows, its rich decoration and its wonderful ornamentation is nothing but a farce in so far as the people of Atlantic Canada are concerned when we have before us a bill for consideration that has already been implemented months ago.
We have not even put it to committee yet. Parliament has not said whether it favours or does not favour the bill. Parliament has not yet said whether this bill ought to be amended, changed substantially or passed exactly as it is. Parliament has made no comment. Yet, the at and east is gone. The new rates for grain have already been implemented and like a crowd of fools, every single one of us, without exception, stands here today and wastes the time and money of the people of Canada.
This Parliament has degenerated into farce under this administration. This bill is the latest example of that contempt for democratic norms being exercised by this government.
You have before you, Mr. Speaker, a question of privilege, a suggestion by a member of this place that the privileges and the rules of this institution have been breached by having this bill come for consideration after the fact.
Mr. Speaker, I respect the position of the Chair. I always, even on those days when I am disappointed with the ruling of the Chair, adhere to that ruling. I submit to you with great respect, Mr. Speaker, that you have before you a question of privilege which we in this party shall support. It is a question of privilege that will not only answer the question of whether or not the government has proceeded properly in bringing us a bill, looking for our approval after the fact, but will determine, in the final analysis, whether the people of Canada should have any respect for this institution whatsoever. It will tell us whether this is nothing but a glorified showcase for partisan points of view on both sides.
It will tell us whether or not, in the last analysis, there is taxation with representation in this land, or whether we have evolved into a presidential style of government where the Prime Minister deigns from time to time to come here and answer a few questions in Question Period. But, otherwise, we have a dictatorial majority government operating with contempt for the views of the

people of Canada and contempt for the properly elected representatives of the people of Canada.
If you listen carefully, Mr. Speaker, you can hear in the silence in this place on occasion when none of us are present, the sound of jackboots.
There is an old saying that Canadians ultimately get the government they deserve. I think Canadians deserve better than this government. Ministers opposite may laugh.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: Well, you're being so foolish.

As they drive around in their chauffeured limousines, and as they leave this place and have their coats passed to them and their boots slipped on by their assistants, and as they are carried off to their offices and told: "Yes, minister, no minister", and brought their cup of tea, and as their hats get increasingly too small and require ever larger pieces of felt to cover their brains, they may believe that they have some divine right to rule unimpeded without the difficulties of dealing with parliamentary tradition and without having to listen to the little people of Canada, who from time to time like to comment on what is happening to them. They may believe that but the people of Canada do not believe that and the people of Canada are not going to stand for this dictatorial politburo-like approach to this country.
It is an incredibly sad day. We have in eastern Europe great reform taking place. We have in eastern Europe celebration of the notion of a multi-party state. They are celebrating the possibility of having governments that are accountable to the people whom supposedly they serve. They are celebrating the possibility of governments which actually may be elected by the people they serve. While no less a person than the Prime Minister celebrates, in his deep melodious tones, this great evolution in eastern Europe, here in this Parliament when rights are squandered, ministers opposite laugh.
Ministers opposite would like to say this is exaggeration. But was it not the Speaker of the Elouse of Commons who was forced to rule only a few months ago that advertising conducted by the government saying: "This is your GST, here is what is going to happen, save this ad" was in contempt of Parliament? Did not the
Speaker of the House of Commons say that that was contemptuous of Parliament and of the people of Canada? Of course he did.
What is the difference between advertising the GST as being passed before it was considered by this place and not just advertising, but implementing, a cancellation of at and east before we have ever seen the bill? The contempt is equal. For the people of Atlantic Canada the ruling of the Chair is fundamental.
It is not fundamental to whether or not Atlantic Canada is going to be treated properly, not to whether there is a sensitivity to the devastating impact of this bill on the region, indeed on farmers in Ontario as well, but to whether this Canada, this federation of peoples and provinces, this experiment in democracy, this lesson to the world of how a nation should govern itself, is as pristine and as pure we would like to believe it is.
Let the government be put on notice that this bill will get no easy ride in this Parliament or in committee. We, in the Liberal Party of Canada, the Official Opposition, I hope joined by my colleagues in the other opposition party, will do everything in our power to ensure that justice is not only done but is seen to be done and that the people of Canada know we will stop this meltdown of our democratic institutions by the government opposite.
What has happened as a result of this bill? First, there was no consultation with the region or with agricultural organizations right across Canada. None whatsoever. What has happened? The Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission recommended changes to the bill, as was pointed out by the member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre. It made recommendations as to how the at and east could save up to 50 per cent of the cost of the program and got absolutely no response from these great believers in democracy opposite. Nothing but the sound of silence followed the recommendation and representations of the business community as represented by the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission in Atlantic Canada. What a singular act of contempt to not even bother to write back and say: "No or yes, bad idea or good idea". There was absolutely nothing. What has happened?

Oh, Mr. Speaker, we have that other great friend of Atlantic Canada, the minister of postal closings, now joining the fray. The minister for privatization and postal closings has just come awake.
Mr. Speaker, what recommendations have been made by the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission? It recommended the use of unit trains from Thunder Bay or direct from prairie origins to move export grain to both Saint John and Halifax. It has asked that the government permit the use of water transport to Halifax and Saint John for Plan C feed grain.
Now get this, Mr. Speaker, the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission has asked for the elimination of the countervail duty on U.S. com. Canada has imposed countervail on U.S. com coming into Canada because that corn is subsidized and we have said that if it is subsidized we are going to put a countervail on it. One result of the actions of this government is there is now an agency in Atlantic Canada lobbying the Government of Canada to take a countervail off U.S. corn, putting our own farmers at a disadvantage as a result, because they are desperate to survive, given the cancellation of the at and east.
What else have they been forced to ask for? They have asked for the provision of permits allowing the importation of feed grains from foreign countries. Atlantic Canadians have been forced, number one, to ask their government to take the countervail off U.S. corn coming into Canada. That is sad, because the at and east is gone. Second, Atlantic Canadians are now asking their government to allow the import of foreign grains into Canada. The government has made the possibility of continuing to be served in Atlantic Canada by Quebec and Ontario so uneconomic, so enviable that we now want to put Canadian farmers out of business by importing foreign grain.
Is that what we want in this country? That is not what we want in Atlantic Canada. Atlantic Canada wants to remain a part of this country and wants to continue to do business with the farmers of Quebec and Ontario. It does not want to lobby for countervail being removed from U.S. products and does not want to import products from outside this country when we can get them right here. When you take a region and cut it off at the knees, when you eliminate a subsidy that makes business possible between Quebec and Ontario, and Atlantic Canada, you
cannot expect people to lie down and play dead. You actually force them to ask for measures that are not in the best interests in the long term of Canada.
I ask this government, for all the reasons I have mentioned, to reconsider this bill, to reconsider the impact on the region and, indeed, on farmers in Quebec and Ontario. I ask this government to withdraw the bill, to have a proper consultation process. I serve notice that failure to do that will meet with an extremely rough ride for this piece of legislation in the appropriate legislative committee, in this case the Standing Committee on Transport.

Mr. Speaker, I must say that I agree entirely with the position taken by the member from Newfoundland. Talk about kicking a victim when it is down. In relation to the real impact of this change, I wonder if the member would comment on the two or three areas he mentioned that are really going to be impacted by the imposition of this change in the at and east rates, and also on the effect of it, not only on the elevators and the flour mills but on other parts of the maritimes as well as the west and Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, I thank the member for his question. I think we could remind ourselves of the stated purpose of this bill when it was introduced by the Hon. Jack Pickersgill, then a Newfoundland member of Parliament, in 1966. He said that the purpose of the at and east was to ensure that eastern Canadian ports could compete with U.S. ports, to enable the ports of Halifax and Saint John to compete with Montreal and other St. Lawrence River ports and to provide for the orderly marketing of grain.

The reality is that in addition to the loss of the elevator at Saint John, which has already been announced, and the loss of the elevator on Georgian Bay at Port McNicoll, it has called into question the continued viability of the elevator and flour mill at Halifax. By extension, it probably will result in increased input costs for farmers in the Atlantic region who, in many instances, are completely on the edge of viability. Another impact that I am sure is not unknown to the government is that with the loss of the at and east subsidy and subsequent loss of business, it is not only probable but likely that we are going to see additional pressure brought to bear by CN and by CP, but primarily by CN, for additional rail line abandonment in Atlantic Canada. With the exception of a couple of runs we have totally lost the VIA Rail traffic. Over the years we have seen the loss of many of the CN freight routes. Newfoundland and P.E.I. are gone entirely. CN has indicated that it wants to abandon more routes.
The loss of the subsidy will increase pressure in that regard as well. Fundamentally the transportation infrastructure of the region, which is sparsely populated but relatively large, is being torn away. Frankly we all know the backbone of any economy, in particular a rural economy, has got to be good transportation infrastructure. That is being destroyed, and this bill contributes significantly to that destruction.

Mr. Speaker, I want to ask my colleague if he has looked at the principle behind this particular bill as being closely related to the Western Grain Transportation Act. Of course in a country as huge, beautiful and diverse as what we have here, the corollary is the huge transportation and shipping costs. Ever since Confederation, and even before that, we have always worked as Canadians to build this country from east to west and to bring in programs that would make one section available to another section. In this case it is to make western grain available to eastern Canada.
I wonder if he sees this particular bill as another move by this administration toward a north-south relationship and to cut Atlantic Canada adrift from the rest of Canada and make it rely on imported grain from the United States or other countries.

Mr. Speaker, I think the hon. member for Lambton-Middlesex said it very well. The fact of the matter is that we have had the movement of western and central Canadian grain into Atlantic Canada. From the west Ontario is the east, but from where I live Ontario is the centre. The loss of the at and east is going to cause that movement to subside substantially.

I do not blame the organization in question. However, I think it is sad when the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission is reduced to petitioning the Government of Canada to remove a countervail that properly has been placed against U.S. com. It is being done not because there is any desire to replace U.S. com with Canadian com, but because the underpinnings, the infrastructure in the region, has been stripped away by this government and the region is desperate.
It is equally sad when the commission, seeing the ability to move western grain into eastern ports being destroyed, is forced to ask the Government of Canada to allow the import of foreign grains over Canadian grains, thus displacing Canadian farmers. It is not done out of any lack of loyalty to the country or out of any lack of desire to continue the trade and commerce between the regions. It is done because there is no choice. Of course we are seeing powerful forces working to increase the north-south pull in the Atlantic regions. There are powerful forces at work in eliminating the east-south trade in the Atlantic region. That cannot be good for national unity.
When we have one region of the country as a consequence of the policy of the government being forced to petition the Government of Canada to remove a countervail on U.S. com, at a time when another region of the country, in this case Ontario farmers, have successfully made a case for that countervail in the first place, then government policies are not contributing to national unity. They are contributing to a set of circumstances which are eating away at the glue that holds the country together and rending the fabric that holds this country together.
What is tragic is that those policies and the effect of those policies are probably not even by design. They are by accident. The government has no idea what it is doing, beyond being concerned about the bottom line and saving, relatively speaking, a pittance. Beyond the bottom line there is no understanding of what the consequences are for Canada and what the impact is on the notion that we live in one country and that we share trade, develop common values, and find ways to bind us together.
This bill contributes toward the destruction of national unity in this country.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to join in the debate this afternoon on Bill C-26, an act to amend the Railway Act, which really boils down to the destruction of the at and east rail freight rate program.
whole communities being destroyed. If we look at the response of groups like the Atlantic farm organizations, we see that they are certainly not pleased with this action by the government.
The members who have spoken before me have outlined some of the problems with this bill, especially with respect to how it impacts on the farmers in Atlantic Canada, on grain elevators in the Georgian Bay ports, and so on.
We have to look at this bill in terms of what the government is doing, that is doing away with unilaterally support programs for agriculture in Canada. That is the genesis of the bill.
The bill really results from a budget last spring which essentially said "we are going to cut government support programs to agriculture". We did not know at that time how devastating those cuts would be because it seemed like the government was talking about $500 million over the next two years. In fact it is much more than that if we count the Western Grain Stabilization Act and the Special Canadian Grains Program, which are needed just as desperately today as they were in the past two or three years. We see that the government is really withdrawing from agriculture to the tune of some $2.5 billion.
This bill before us today is part of that act of withdrawing some $500 million. The actual cost of the support program for grain and flour transportation under the at and east is some $60 million.
If we look at our competition, the people with whom we compete in the world, we see the United States increasing its support programs for transportation, loan rates for grains and so on, but most of all support programs for exports. Some $900 million will be provided in support programs to take away markets from Canadian producers in Russia, China, the Middle East, Africa and so on. The United States is continuing to wage war on Canadian agricultural producers. This support program is only one small part of that withdrawal by the government, but it is certainly important to our producers. It is extremely important to Atlantic farmers and to the Atlantic economy.
This is at a time when the Atlantic economy is being slaughtered not only by government programs but by the government's maintenance of the fishery. We see nightly on television those programs being withdrawn. We see
As I said, this measure involves only some $60 million, but it is a very important support program. It is part of that $500 million that was withdrawn which involves crop insurance, $200 million; the rail branch line rehabilitation program, $48 million; grain and crop advance payment program, for which we fought hard in the House last fall; the dairy export program; the commodity based loan program; the Canadian Dairy Commission program; and the rebate on fuel tax for agriculture amounting to $500 million over the next two years.
We keep hearing that the incoming budget is to be even more Draconian than the one we have seen so far.
After I read this in the budget I had an opportunity to hear representations from the Maritime Farmers Council. The council wrote a letter to me in June of this year in which it estimates that the additional cost for livestock and poultry milling wheat will be some $9,120,000 or $21 per tonne for the 400,000 tonnes of prairie grain and Ontario com which is imported into the Atlantic region each year.
I wrote to the Minister of Agriculture to ask him to withdraw this action in view of the very adverse impact it would have on Canadian agriculture, especially in Atlantic Canada. It was very interesting that the minister took several months to reply. When he did he simply said that the program was not necessary any longer and that it no longer serves its original purpose. Thus the decision was made to conclude it as of July 15. Several members have already argued strenuously that that is a unilateral decision. The legislation is there. The government has no authority to withdraw its legislation on the books. It should not be withdrawn.
Interestingly enough, I wrote back to the minister and said clearly that one of the original purposes of the program was to assist Atlantic farmers in having a more realistic price for their livestock feeds. The minister wrote back and said he recognized that the maintenance of water transportation of feed grain in the Atlantic region was crucial and that the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds would be announcing measures to

that effect in the near future. That was in a letter from the Minister of Agriculture on December 13.

One begins to wonder whether there is anything there. It is my understanding that already the Saint John elevator has signalled its closure. One wonders whether Halifax can be far behind.
With regard to additional costs of livestock and poultry feed, I have already mentioned that the impact of that is outlined by the farm groups in Atlantic Canada at some $9.12 million. That is a major new cost to those producers. The minister has said: "We are going to announce some program to compensate for that". He has turned that over to the Minister of State for Grains and Oilseeds and so far there has been no announcement in that regard. Not only do we see a reduced economic impact in Atlantic Canada, but we see hardship for the agricultural producers there.

National Defence installations. The total economic impact of this support program is some $27 million, which is an estimate by the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission.
We see a Draconian measure here that not only has an extremely adverse impact on agriculture in Atlantic Canada but on the general economy in the port cities of Saint John and Halifax.
This is a general withdrawal by the government of its support programs. I do not think there has ever been a time in our history when agriculture has faced such dismal prospects in terms of net farm income or uncertainty due to the government's actions.
If we look at the net farm income for the prairie provinces, we see that next year Saskatchewan faces a negative net farm income of some $9 million, down from over $1 billion in this past year. The government, in its Green Paper on agriculture, has said that its policy is to remove support programs. We have seen this in the budget. This measure is part of the program to open up markets and to destroy marketing boards.
Interestingly enough, the government talks about regional sensitivity. Nothing could be further from the truth. If we destroy marketing boards, as is certainly in the cards judging by the way the government is moving, the dairy and poultry industries in Atlantic Canada will surely be destroyed. The same is true if we take away support programs like the at and east rate which is so helpful in terms of transportation.
This bill is part of an over-all scheme of the government as outlined in its Green Paper, which will be extremely harmful to all parts of the country.
Today in the House the Minister of Agriculture was talking about what action he would take under the free trade deal. Clearly the relationship with the United States, our largest trading partner in agriculture, has never been in such a deplorable state. We have the Secretary of Agriculture, Mr. Yeutter, providing some $900 million in the export enhancement program to steal away markets from Canadian agricultural wheat and grain producers in western Canada. He is providing subsidies of $20 a tonne and more to those markets in China and Russia which are our traditional customers.

If we look at Article 701.4 of the free trade deal we see that it states:
Each Party shall take into account the export interests of the other
Party in the use of any export subsidy on any agricultural goods
exported to third countries, recognizing that such subsidies may have
prejudicial effects on the export interests of the other Party.
That is what I am talking about.
The U.S. is putting in place a $900 million export subsidy program while we are removing support programs for our industry. What could be more absurd than the actions we see? Clearly the government is unilaterally pulling away the underpinning, the support programs, while at the same time the Americans are dramatically reinforcing and increasing their programs over the next seven years to the tune of almost a billion dollars.
We do not only have to look at the grain industry which includes wheat, barley and other grain commodities for which our markets are being raided by the United States. Let us look at the arrangement we have seen in the pork countervail case of last September. The Prime Minister promised that the United States countervail law, the dumping duty law, could not apply to Canada, period. Nothing could be further from the truth.
Last September the United States imposed a countervail duty which in 15 months' time could be increased dramatically from 8 cents a kilo to two or three times that as a result of our support programs in Canada. We see an industry which is in very severe decline because of the threat of that countervail. The Prime Minister's promise that the United States trade law could not apply to Canada, period, is really hollow to those producers.
In the Green Paper the minister talks about regional sensitivity and about maintaining a viable agricultural industry in Atlantic Canada. If the decision on ice cream and yogurt brought down by the GATT panel last November and accepted by this government is implemented at the end of the GATT negotiations this year, clearly our whole market for processed dairy products- some 60 per cent of our entire production-will be open to imports from the United States. This will have a very adverse negative impact on regional agriculture, especially in Ontario and Quebec but just as much in Atlantic Canada.
The Minister of Agriculture in a speech he made last week complained about harassment by the United States of our beef industry and our exports to the United States. The U.S. government has dramatically increased the number of inspections of our exports. He talked about increasing the inspection fees in the U.S. from $100 to $700.
The free trade deal was supposed to solve the problems caused by non-tariff barriers, export enhancement subsidies, and pork countervail. It was supposed to preserve supply management and marketing boards. Clearly none of that has happened.
Our trade problems in agriculture have increased dramatically. The United States is demanding total access to our markets, for example in the area of ice cream and yogurt, markets to which it has not had access before because of tariffs. Those tariffs are coming off. At the same time the U.S. is restricting access to its markets, whether it is in pork, beef or whatever.
We have a government that is unilaterally cutting its own throat, cutting the throat of agriculture in Canada, by reducing support programs while at the same time the United States is dramatically increasing its support programs. It is little wonder that agriculture in this country is facing the greatest uncertainty that it ever has in the past.
The government has fumbled the ball in the free trade deal. Everything is falling apart under that arrangement-the marketing boards, the countervails on pork and the export subsidies on grain by the U.S. The bill before us tonight is part of a decline in support for agriculture at a time when the industry desperately needs the support. While we are cutting back unilaterally the United States and other countries are maintaining their full force in support of agriculture.
The disturbing part is that this comes at an adverse time both for our exporters and for Atlantic Canada. While they are facing perhaps one of the worst economic crises in their history, the government is withdrawing its support not only in economic terms for the grain industry and flour industry in Saint John and Halifax but as well for the agricultural producers.
We are opposed to this legislation. We intend to oppose it in every way possible. It is unilateral action which is not being matched by our trading partners, by the United States, even though we have signed a free trade deal which is supposed to guarantee that we will

co-operate. We are co-operating. We are unilaterally removing support programs while at the same time the U.S. is increasing its support programs to take away world markets and to support its own producers.

Mr. Speaker, the at and east rate is relative to the freight rates to some extent from Boston east. It was brought in, in 1959, to make sure that grains used by the flour industry, and to some extent by the people involved in the movement of flour, and the poultry and hog industry as well, be bought through Canadians instead of Americans.

I would like the member to comment on whether or not this is really any different from the original need, which was to get the eastern provinces to buy Ontario and western grain for their needs.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Saskatoon-Humboldt. Clearly, as he mentioned, this support program is very important to Atlantic Canada. Mr. Speaker, I think that is extremely important. If free market forces solve regional development problems in this country, they would have been solved already. That is why I believe that the minister's green paper on the future of agriculture is really unbelievable. He says that we are going to remove support programs unilaterally. The dairy and poultxy industry and other industries hardly exist there because there is no system to encourage them to produce and be viable.

Mr. Speaker, this is not the first time I have had to speak on transportation programs such as the at and east rate for various regions in Canada. History tells us that the reason it is called the at and east rate is that it is based on what the American railroads were doing from Buffalo east to the Atlantic coast ports in the United States. Hence their name "at and east", the ports from Lake Huron, Georgian Bay, the upper and lower St. Lawrence and the Atlantic provinces.
Mr. Speaker, I want to submit to you, Sir, and I hope you will raise this matter in consultations that will go on, that this should not be dealt with in this House until the Speaker of the House of Commons and the National Transportation Agency have ruled on the action of the government. This would be a ruling by the Chair. The action of the railways should be the subject of a ruling of the National Transportation Agency, before which there is now an application on the implementation of the Railway Act.
Since last summer, the government has disobeyed the law of the land. The railways have ceased collecting and the railroads have been charging those who formerly got the benefits of the at and east rates, that is the full commercial rate in violation of the Railway Act. The government has ordered the railroads to do that. The government has not put up a single nickel since last summer. The legislation has not passed second reading, let alone receive Royal Assent. If there was ever a travesty of the parliamentary and democratic process, this is another one.
The Chair ruled recently about government advertising of legislation that had not passed Parliament. That was to spend money. This time the government is breaking the law of the land to save some money at the expense of western grain producers, the Atlantic provinces and Great Lakes ports. In my opinion, there can be no doubt the Chair must rule that the government must cease and desist in implementing what this bill requires before it becomes an act of Parliament. If we have to take the National Transportation Agency to court for not implementing the Railway Act, so be it. We will see this government in court because it is that serious.

I hope, Sir, that you will ask your colleagues, the Clerk and Clerk Assistants, to take this into consideration. I have been here for the same length of time as you have, Mr. Speaker, quite a while, and I do not recall the government implementing a law before it has been passed by Parliament. The government has become a little worried about it and has requested the railroads to keep track of it all, just in case it is found to be like a sick bird, illegal.
I know, Mr. Speaker, you would like to bring in a substitute but I wanted to get that word in to you before you did.
My final point on this is that the government in fact has advertised this legislation by ordering it to be carried out before it was passed.
Another point I want to make is that the bill is wrong in principle because it flies in the face of what this country has done since before 1867. Our forefathers took into account the whole settlement of the nation. They took into account our geography, our climate and where our people were located and where they produced and processed their goods. That is why there was the Crow's Nest Pass agreement of 1897.
That is why there were subsequently programs such as the bridge rates to get goods across northern Ontario where, at that time, there were very few people living. The trains did not need to stop and start up very often. There was no St. Lawrence Seaway. Subsequently, there was the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act, the Maritime Freight Rates Act, and the at and east rates which are now almost one-quarter of a century old. All of these programs should be looked at every five years or so and assessed as to how well they are doing and what improvements might be made. Nobody is suggesting they are perfect. The problem is, whenever a government says it is time to review something, it sure as heck does not review it to improve it. It reviews it to get rid of it and the government does not consult with the people who depend on that program.
Another reason for these programs was to protect ourselves from what the Americans were doing, then and now. Halifax and Saint John are two of the very few ice-free ports that we have. I guess one could add a couple or three more such as Vancouver, Prince Rupert

and New Westminster. We could add Saint John, but they took away the railroad. You do not truck grain that far for export, milling wheat or flour. You cannot count Saint John. So Halifax and Saint John are the only two that are ice-free.
The Americans will be increasing the Export Enhancement Program from approximately $530 million to $900 million in their next budget. What does the government do to protect Canadians in a region of Canada that has already suffered too much? It cancelled one of the few remaining programs they have. It means something to the ports of Halifax and Saint John, to the feed grain producers in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, and to the milling industry in Halifax and Ontario.
We used to have half a dozen or more flour mills in the prairie provinces and we have lost all but one or two of them. We should be processing our production right where we produce it. We send it away because of some misbegotten principle that an end product costs more to move than a bulk product. I have never believed that even from my first days on the railroad and neither did my father before me.
I remember receiving a cabinet document in a plain brown envelope in 1981. I had a press conference in Regina and one here in Ottawa. This document outlined a long term policy. That was under a Liberal government, but it outlined the long-term policy that over a number of years, the government would get out from under every single transportation assistance program. It has continued in progression ever since then.
When we were in the Atlantic provinces dealing with deregulation and some of my colleagues were there dealing with the free trade deal, and when we held hearings on the Crow rate debate in 1982 and 1983, we warned the people of the Atlantic provinces. I suppose one of the saddest experiences I have ever gone through in the House of Commons is seeing the Hon. Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Agriculture. He and I sat together hour after hour, week after week, and year after year fighting together against what he and his government are doing now. He is a good friend and another member of the class of 1968.1 say to myself in sadness and sorrow: "Where the hell is he now?"
There is more to this than the government saving an average of $32 million a year. That is what the average cost of the at and east rates has been. It has to do with our whole nationhood. It has to do with the west and it has to do with the Atlantic provinces. When one of us gets hurt, all the rest of us get hurt either then or later. It has happened ad nauseam over the last 20 years. To rebuild the economy in the Atlantic provinces and on the prairies, we have to keep the present programs, improve them and enlarge them. The principle is that the nation as a whole shares in the cost of our nationhood. We do not victimize one province or one region because we have to reduce the budget and the deficit.
We will oppose this bill in principle because it has no principles. It flies in the face of the principles of our nation and our history. The government thinks it is going to save $32 million a year. What it will cost in unemployment insurance, severance pay and a host of other things for the 500 or 600 people who are employed directly or indirectly in Halifax and Saint John, plus the cost to the railroads, intermediate ports and terminals-Midland, Ontario, for example-western grain producers and how much more it will cost the Canadian Wheat Board to export our milling grain and flour will be more, much more than $32 million. It is a false economy and it hurts Canadians. It hurts Canadians in the areas who have already been hurt too much.
The Crow's Nest Pass and bridge rates are gone. The government has been niggling away at the Maritime Freight Rates Act and the Atlantic Region Freight Assistance Act. We have lost more than 3,000 miles of branch-lines and now it is hitting Quebec, Ontario and the Atlantic provinces. Two provinces, Newfoundland and P.E.I., will have no railroad at all. We lost the two-price wheat. We lost interest-free cash advances. And the government brags about how much it has done for agriculture. With friends like that, I wish they would go away.
There used to be a three-way deal. The Soviet Union would sign a contract for one, two or three million tonnes of Canadian grain. It was assisting Cuba. It asked Canada to mill a certain portion of that grain into flour and ship it to Cuba. The Cubans, who did not have dollars or roubles, sent the equivalent value in sugar and rum to the Soviet Union. The Soviet Union paid us in cash. It worked for several years as a beautiful three-way deal. Dover Flour Mills in Halifax milled a lot of that flour. A lot of it was milled in mills in Ontario and in Montreal. We even shipped some from Saskatoon. That is gone. It is down the drain.
Then one hears about the additional subsidy and export enhancement which will bring the American subsidy up to as much as $30 a tonne depending on the kind and quality of grain. One hears about people in Atlantic Canada saying in desperation that it would be cheaper for us to import seed grain from Europe. My God, what are we doing? We are debating the same nonsense we started with the unlamented Otto Lang, only these guys are doing it in spades.
There is the other problem called harmonization. The government is so desperate to make sure that the United States is happy with us under the free trade agreement that we do not want to hurt their feelings. It considers the Canadian Wheat Board, the at and east rates, and our standards on plywood to be unfair. As a result this government is bringing in legislation and regulations, not to benefit Canada, but to bring us into line with the wishes of the United States government and United States Congress. There can be no doubt about that.
It used to be a firing-squad offence things for traitorous behaviour and for cowardice in the face of the enemy. In this case they talk about the economic enemy and, for that matter, a social enemy. In other ways they are good friends. The Americans are angry at us for one of the rare occasions we put a countervail on U.S. com.

It is coming into Ontario mainly, and a little into Quebec, at outrageously subsidized prices and they are complaining.
I urge the Chair to say this bill cannot be dealt with until the government enforces the law this bill is trying to change. One cannot make the law and a bill like this retroactive. It is rare when that happens and budget bills are among the few in which it does happen. We also have to wait until the National Transportation Agency rules on their jurisdiction being usurped, preventing them from implementing the Railway Act, enforcing the Railway Act on both Canadian railways.

Mr. Speaker, back in the early 1970s and the late 1960s a group of farmers and transportation people took the government department to court regarding the temporary reserves act and won that particular case. Would the Hon. Member for Regina-Lumsden, who was in the House at that time, comment on the circumstances under which that case was brought to court and what happened.

I am glad my colleague for Saskatoon- Humboldt reminded me. It was in 1970 or 1971 that the then minister brought in a bill called, "Lower Inventories for Tomorrow". Imagine paying farmers not to grow food, if that was not stupid enough. In the bill was a clause that repealed the temporary Wheat Reserves Act retroactively for 18 months. So that is not the first time I have seen this retroactive nonsense. We checked with some legal eagles and we were told that I could not take the government to court, the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool and the farmer's union could not take them to court, that it had to be somebody who had a direct interest in the matter.
The temporary Wheat Reserves Act was a measure whereby, if there was more that a certain amount of grain in store at the end of a crop year, and I think the ceiling was 175 million bushels, for anything more than that the federal government paid the storage costs. It was not the farmer's fault that the Seaway was frozen. It was not the farmer's fault that international markets had gone to hell. The government protected them. They tried to retroactively cancel the temporary Wheat Reserves Act, and the government had not sent a nickel to the Canadian Wheat Board for 18 months. It came to
Government Orders
nice tidy figure of a little over $96 million that the government of day owed to the Canadian Wheat Board.
We did some more inquiring. I got a well-to-do farmer and a poor farmer and a couple of middle-sized farmers in my hon. friend's constituency that used to be called Assiniboia, in the area in Milestone, and we took them to Federal Court. The Deputy Minister of Justice, the judge, the interpreters, the whole works had to be flown to Regina. God knows what that cost. The Minister of Justice of the day, the most recent leader of the official opposition, and the Minister of Finance of the day were ready to shoot one Otto Lang, only nobody would let them have a gun.
We not only won the $96 million, we won $1.7 in interest charges. Then we won another $2,700 in court costs. I was a little worried about who was going to put up the court costs, but we won it. Why? Because the government of that day attempted to retroactively prevent their agencies from enforcing the law that the Parliament of Canada had passed. That is exactly what is being attempted now. By the way, we did not get an injunction. We applied for and got a writ of mandamus, which is the opposite of an injunction. An injunction states that you cannot do something. A writ of mandamus states that you must do something. In that instance it was: "You must obey your own law". Mr. Speaker, this government must obey its own law.
It is bad enough that they bring this bill in to take effect today without royal assent. But to bring it in retroactive for 18 months-and it will be that much, at least-but if it ever gets through here, it is the same principle. That flies in the face of a democratic system. It flies in the face of the principle that the first one to obey the law is the government itself.
I always thought that might be a lesson for years to come for any government of any political stripe. Obviously, it has not been. If we have to go through that exercise again, so be it.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise to speak on Bill C-26, an act to amend the Railway Act, regarding grain and flour subsidies.
This legislation proposes to eliminate the at and east subsidies for the transport of export grain and flour through eastern Canadian ports. The elimination of

Government Orders
business for our ports is the last thing Atlantic Canada needs in these difficult times.
The at and east program has been in effect since the 1960s. It was intended to offset some of the economic advantages that the U.S. eastern ports had over Canadian ports in terms of proximity to the sources of grain supply, larger facilities, and better transportation services.
Under the program, a fixed rate level for the movement of grain and flour from western Canada by rail to eastern ports was established in order to encourage the use of the eastern ports. Because the rail rates were frozen by statute, the railways were reimbursed by the federal government for the difference between the fixed rates charged to grain and flour shippers and the actual rates normally charged by the railways and set by the National Transportation Agency.
The at and east program has had far-reaching and beneficial effects on eastern ports, especially those of Halifax and Saint John and, therefore, on the regional economy. Almost 100 per cent of all export grain tonnage shipped through Saint John, and approximately 60 per cent of tonnage by way of Halifax, moved under the at and east rates. The direct and indirect benefits of such a huge amount of tonnage moving through our eastern ports are vital to the region's economy. The loss of this business will be devastating.
In its budget of 1989, the federal government announced the intention to eliminate the at and east grain and flour subsidy. The government's rationale for killing the subsidy was that the cost of shipping by rail to the U.S. ports is now considerably higher than it was at the time of the program's initiation, and that the railway costs were higher than those of shipping by water through the St. Lawrence Seaway. Also, the government stated that the subsidy created distortions and inefficiencies in the movement of grain and that the subsidy is: "Inconsistent with the government's market-oriented transportation policy."
We in Atlantic Canada know all to well that this government is market-oriented rather than people-oriented. The elimination of this program is going to have a devastating effect not only on the ports of Halifax and Saint John, but on the entire maritime region. The first to suffer will be the workers whose jobs depend on the
grain and flour that moves on Canadian railways and through those ports.
We in Atlantic Canada have suffered through a year of negative government policies which are already having a devastating effect on the Atlantic economy, policies such as the closure and reduction of Canadian Armed Forces bases, the ongoing crisis in the Atlantic fishery, the gutting of the unemployment insurance program, and the cut-backs in VIA Rail. As if this were not enough, the government is now going to ruin the vital Saint John and Halifax ports which will have terrible direct and indirect consequences.
An analysis by the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission estimated that approximately $14.5 million in economic activity will be lost to the Atlantic region by the elimination of the at and east rail rates. If the Saint John and Halifax elevators were to close, the cost could reach approximately $26.5 million. The region cannot bear this kind of blow, especially now with a terrible year behind us, an even a worse one to come, and a recession looming.
The impact will be felt by the ports and by other sectors of the economy that depend on the movement of grain through the ports such as the activity in the grain elevators in Saint John and Halifax, and employment in the ports and on the railway. Indeed, the effect is already being felt. Even though this House did not pass the legislation, the National Transportation Agency has, without the approval of the House of Commons, raised the rates charged on export grain and flour moving on Canadian railways to eastern ports. It is no coincidence that the grain elevator at Saint John is slated to close this month, and that is only the beginning.
What would happen if the elevator in Halifax were to close? Beside its role in the movement of export grain, the elevator plays an important role in the storage and handling of domestic feed grain, and milling wheat. The elevators' inability to store and handle these grains, or even a rise in costs, would seriously damage the Atlantic pork, poultry, egg, and beef industries.
In addition, the Halifax elevator is the sole means of storage for milling wheat for the only Atlantic regional flour mill. The loss of the Halifax storage facility, which would result in large increases in freight rates and major capital expenditures for new or upgraded facilities,

would seriously damage the competitiveness of the flour mill.
As if the effect on the ports, elevators and mills is not bad enough, the maritimes would face the abandonment of much more of the rail network in a region which depends on the movement of grain and flour to the ports. It is painfully obvious that the elimination of the at and east transport subsidies would have a devastating impact on the economy of the Atlantic region which is already reeling from the effects of other government policies.
Employment will feel the pinch. The people who depend on a healthy, viable port industry will be among the first to suffer as jobs begin to disappear in the ports, the elevators, and the railways.
After the government announced that the at and east subsidy would be eliminated, the president of the Halifax grain elevator estimated that several hundred jobs could be lost at the port of Halifax as a direct result of this decision.
The estimate did not include the number of jobs lost in related sectors. Industry and labour officials all predict the major loss of business and jobs in the ports, elevators, and related industries as a result of higher transportation rates.
The Atlantic region cannot bear this loss of yet more jobs. How many times do we have to tell that to this government? When will it begin to understand the ultimate cost of its negative, short-sighted policies? Atlantic Canadians want to work. They need to work. They do not want to depend on unemployment insurance, or what will be left of the program if the government gets its way. Hundreds of jobs depend directly and indirectly on healthy, viable ports, elevators and grain transportation systems. The long-term costs of the loss of these jobs and of the damage to the Atlantic economy caused by an under-utilization of these systems and facilities will be enormous.
It is only logical that if there is a loss of government support for the transport of grain and flour along Canadian railways to eastern Canadian ports, less grain and flour will move through the ports. The Atlantic region already suffers from inherent disadvantages in competing with the U.S. ports which enjoy better ship-
Govemment Orders
ping connections, not only with the American grain producers, but to the Canadian producers as well.
It is an age-old problem for eastern ports. The at and east helped us to remain competitive with the U.S. I should note that the at and east not only helped the eastern sector of grain and flour movement, but the western sector as well. Wheat boards need the fixed rates to move grain during the winter months to offset the higher costs of rail movement after the Seaway navigation closes. They need the fixed rates in order to sustain shipment to customers on a year-round basis.
By the elimination of the subsidies, the government manages to hurt both the eastern and western economies. If the government is truly concerned about reducing the amount of money it pays for the subsidies, while allowing the ports to remain viable, why has it not even responded to the positive proposals put forth by the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission?
As long ago as 1985, as was mentioned earlier this afternoon, at the invitation of the Minister of Transport, the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission submitted proposals to make the at and east more efficient. The commission acknowledged that the program, as it was originally planned, did eventually create some distortions in the movement of grain by discouraging the use of least cost routing.
But the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission believes that it is possible to be cost efficient, while still meeting certain objectives. Those objectives are to maintain the grain elevators at Saint John and Halifax, to maintain the commercial viability of the Halifax flour mill, and to maintain a constant flow of grain by rail through the two ports.
The APTC proposed that the frozen rates to the St. Lawrence ports be raised to compensatory levels and be held at such levels by the NTA. At the same time, the rates to eastern ports would be set at a fixed differential over the compensatory rates which would maintain the competitive relationship between the St. Lawrence and the Atlantic ports.
Finally, the APTC recommended that the fixed rates to Atlantic ports also apply to water transport, which is the most cost-efficient method of grain movement, and that the federal government fund a marine receiving
