Government Orders
facility at Saint John. The port currently has no such facility and can therefore handle only rail deliveries.
It was estimated that the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission proposal would have resulted in government savings of some $22 million in transportation subsidies per year, which is about one-half of the total cost of the at and east program. But the Atlantic Province Transportation Commission never received a government response to its proposals. It seems that the efficient movement of grain to eastern ports, with the least amount of damage to western and eastern economies, is not the government's primary concern. Well, the government is once again bowing down to its idol of market-oriented policy while disregarding the human costs.
Atlantic Canadian workers asked the government to reconsider its short-sighted decision to completely eliminate the at and east program. They asked the government to consult with groups such as the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission so that the current distortions in the system could be eliminated without destroying the viability of Atlantic ports. With effort, ingenuity, and some will on the part of the government it can be done.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to say that it is a pleasure for me to take part in this debate today because it is not. The debate should not even be happening, if the government had any sense of justice or any sense of fairness. I am going to put forth a few ideas, most of which are not mine, but which come through my reading of the brief prepared by the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission.
According to APTC, the termination of the at and east rates will have serious economic consequences for the maritime ports, as well as certain activities that depend on the movement of export grain and flour through those ports. Based on an estimate made by the commission, the economic impact of the at and east rates program on the Atlantic provinces, based on 1985 data, was close to $35 million annually.
In addition to this, several studies have shown that the at and east structure, in its present form, creates certain distortions and inefficiencies in the movement of export grain and flour. In recognition of possible distortions, in
1985 the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission proposed certain modifications in the program to first reduce the demand on the federal treasury, second, lessen or eliminate distortions and inefficiencies, and third, to maintain movement of export grain and flour through Atlantic ports. The objectives of the proposed modifications were the maintenance of the grain elevators as viable units at Halifax and Saint John, the maintenance of the commercial viability of the flour mill at Halifax, and maintaining a flow of export grain and flour through Atlantic ports.
The specific proposal of the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission was that the rates be frozen at the present level, and the St. Lawrence ports be allowed to raise to a compensatory level and be held at a compensatory level on an annual basis by the national government. The economic impact of the government proposal on the Atlantic region will be in excess of $34 million.
An analysis by the APTC of the regional impact of the program showed that approximately $14.4 million in economic activity will be lost to the region due to the termination of this subsidy. However, should both grain elevators in the region at Halifax and Saint John be unable to continue operations, then the negative impact would amount to approximately $27.6 million. These amounts do not include any economic activity generated by the program which occurred outside the Atlantic region, such as railway employment, inland elevators, lake vessels, et cetera.
The maintenance of the Halifax grain elevators as a viable operation is of critical economic import to the entire Atlantic region. As well as the activity generated by the movement of export grain through the facility, the elevator also plays a vital role in the storage and handling of domestic feed grain and milling wheat.
Local pork, poultry and egg industries and, to a lesser extent, the beef industry, would be seriously affected should the Halifax elevator be unable to remain in operation. That is very dicey. In addition, the Halifax elevator is utilized as the only means of storage for milling wheat by the Atlantic region flour mill. The use of the Halifax elevator for domestic feed grains represents the only competitive alternative to the use of the railways as a means of obtaining the required feed
February 12, 1990

ingredients for the local livestock and poultry industries as well.
The use of lake vessels to Halifax with truck delivery beyond is the only competition faced by the railways for the amount of domestic feed grains into the maritimes. Without this alternative, rail rates for the domestic feed grains would be higher than presently is the case. As evidence of this fact, one has only to look at the historical record of feed grain rates to the maritimes to see that a significant drop in the rail rates took place when the water route to Halifax and the Halifax elevator began to be utilized for the handling of domestic livestock feed grains.
The local livestock and poultry industries in the maritimes face a tremendous disadvantage in terms of feed costs versus their competition in Quebec and Ontario. Any feed cost increases would place these industries in jeopardy. Local feed grain production in the maritimes meets approximately 20 per cent of requirements in Nova Scotia, from 35 to 40 per cent in New Brunswick, and up to 80 per cent in Prince Edward Island. The flour mill at Halifax faces intense competition in the Atlantic provinces market from competitors located in central Canada. It is totally dependent on the Halifax elevator for storage of milling wheat. The loss of that storage facility resulting in large increases in freight rates and capital expenditure to construct alternative storage facilities would seriously erode the competitiveness of the local mill. Local milling wheat producers would be faced with the loss of their only market should the flour mill at Halifax be abandoned or unable to continue operations.
In addition, the only source for mill feeds within the region would disappear resulting in higher procurement costs for the feed industry and higher feed prices. The Saint John grain elevator serves only the export market, however, the rail traffic provided by the movement of export grain over that portion of the rail line from Montreal to Saint John was an important contribution to the viability of that line. The maritimes is dealing with the abandonment of approximately 50 per cent of the rail network in the region. Any loss of traffic which will affect the viability of remaining lines is viewed as a very serious matter.
The shipment of export flour through the port of Halifax contributed significantly to employment at the port. It also played an important role for the railways in
Government Orders
the positioning of boxcars within the maritimes for domestic use as the cars utilizing the shipment of export flour to Halifax were then positioned within the maritimes for the shipment of domestic cargo such as newsprint.
In 1985, in response to an invitation from the Minister of Transport, the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission developed and submitted specific proposals designed to make the at and east subsidy program more effective and efficient, while at the same time ensuring that the program responded to three regional economic objectives. These objectives were to maintain the grain elevators at Halifax and Saint John as viable units, to maintain the commercial viability of the flour mill at Halifax, and to maintain a constant flow of export grain and flour by rail through the ports of Halifax and Saint John.
The APTC proposal called for the rail rates on export grain and flour to St. Lawrence River ports to rise to compensatory levels. Rates to maritime ports would then be maintained at a fixed differential in relation to the St. Lawrence ports to allow the maritime ports to continue to participate in the movement of this traffic. The subsidy would maintain the fixed differential in rates. The proposal also called for the application of the program to include the use of water transportation to the maritime ports, and for the federal government to provide funding for a marine receiving facility for grain at Saint John to enable the use of water transportation to that port and to reduce the level of subsidy that would otherwise be required to support the use of higher cost rail transportation.
It was agreed by all parties that steps must be taken to ensure that the grain elevators at Halifax and Saint John are able to continue as viable operations, and that export grain and flour continue to move through the ports of Halifax and Saint John. They have put forward proposals with the Atlantic Provinces Transportation Commission to minimize harmful effects. The problem is the government does not listen.
The use of unit trains from Thunder Bay, or direct from prairie origins, to move export grain to both Saint John and Halifax is viable. This would allow both railroads to establish rates based on their most efficient method of operation. However, to become a viable alternative, this would require the full support of the Canadian Wheat Board and a commitment to provide existing government-owned covered hopper cars under

February 12, 1990
Government Orders
the same terms as they are provided under the Western Grain Transportation Act. Wouldn't that be terrible!
To permit the use of water transportation to Halifax and Saint John for Plan C feed grain would allow the most economical mode of transportation to be utilized for grain movement under Plan C pricing. The elimination of the countervail duty on U.S. corn would allow the elevators at Saint John and Halifax the opportunity to utilize existing back-haul vessel capacity to receive U.S. corn from Atlantic seaboard ports. The local livestock industry could then have the option of securing its corn requirements from either Canadian or U.S. sources, depending upon market conditions, and providing throughout at the local elevators.
The provision of facilities to receive grain by water at the Saint John grain elevator is currently unable to function due to the lack of necessary marine unloading equipment. Imagine how long they would put up with that in one of the Great Lakes seaports. The provision of equipment to allow for the receiving of grain by water would give the elevator the opportunity to solicit business, which it is not able to accommodate at present, such as U.S. corn or shipments of Canadian export grain directly from lake vessels.
What of the continued use of Halifax for the shipment of export flour? The natural advantages of Halifax for the handling of this type of cargo should be promoted and fully utilized. Another proposal is the provision of permits allowing the importation of feed grains from foreign countries. This would allow the grain elevators at Halifax and Saint John to increase the volume of grain handled, should opportunities arise in this market and contribute to the over-all viability of the operations.
The at and east export grain and flour subsidy program had important implications for several domestic industries in the Atlantic region, including local livestock producers, flour milling and the railways. With the cancellation of this program, the continued viability of grain elevators at Halifax and Saint John is definitely in jeopardy.
It is vital that these and other alternatives put forth by other interested parties be examined and a solution found to guarantee the continued operation of the grain elevators at Halifax and Saint John.
Despite the woeful contempt of this government for Parliament, I am making this proposal developed by the APTC in the vain hope that this government may listen to reasonable and thoughtful alternatives. However, these are the same people who have not listened to any other proposals that'have been put forward. I ask, indeed I plead with the government to listen and seriously consider the well-being of Atlantic Canada. We are still a part of this nation. We have not been cut adrift yet, although the government has worked very hard at doing that.
While the Prime Minister, the Minister for International Trade, the Minister of National Defence, the Minister of Employment and Immigration, and the Minister of Finance are all busy trying to savage our social programs, our military bases, our fisheries and our way of life, what are our Atlantic Tory members doing? Where is the Minister of Veterans Affairs hiding? Where is the Minister of Regional Development? What is he doing?
What can we expect of these people who have betrayed their mandate and their people? These are the same people who silently allowed the government to savage Atlantic Canada after we had the Wilsonian restraint. These are the same people who have allowed our military bases to be savaged throughout Atlantic Canada and elsewhere.
These are the same people who silently allowed Canada Post to ride roughshod over the will of the people. That is another dictatorship in this country.
The clock is ticking and Atlantic Canadians have long, long memories. I say to my colleagues opposite that the time is running out for them. It is time to start fighting for your region, for the infrastructure, what is left of it and, most of all, for your people.
Atlantic Canadians are getting very fed up with this government. They are sick and tired of being betrayed. Every promise that was made to Atlantic Canadians has been broken. I cannot think of one promise that was made, and there were a lot of them in the last couple of elections. I cannot think of one that has not been broken. It is time members of this government started to be a
February 12, 1990

little sensible and a little sensitive to the people of Atlantic Canada. If they are not they will pay the price, because Atlantic Canadians have very long memories.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, is the hon. member aware that the federal government, through the Atlantic Opportunities Agency, has spent over a billion dollars and that there will be new co-operative agreements emerging? Is he aware that since 1984 the federal government has spent $540 million in Cape Breton alone? Is he aware that unemployment in the Atlantic provinces since this present government has been in power has fallen enormously from 1984? Is he aware that unemployment has fallen in every province of Atlantic Canada since this government has been in power, compared to the previous government?
Is he aware of these very important facts which indicate the strength of commitment, resolve and the practical contribution that the federal government has exhibited toward Atlantic Canada right from the first month of its mandate?

Now, Mr. Speaker, that is what you call looking at the world through rose-coloured glasses. As a matter of fact I would say blue-coloured glasses.
Let me tell the hon. member what I remember. I remember the betrayal of CFB Chatham and the directorate of pay services. I remember the betrayal of myriad promises that were made throughout Atlantic Canada. I can see what is happening to CFB Summerside: another betrayal.
I can go on and on, but you have the picture, Mr. Speaker. You can talk about CN shops too, if you want. You can talk about the refusal of this government to enter into a cost sharing agreement with the Atlantic provinces to maintain their infrastructure.
That is nothing new.
No, it is nothing new, but the government had been out of power so long that we forgot how very bad it could be.

Certainly, I think a very strong case could be made for

Mr. Speaker, I rise yet again in this Elouse more in sorrow than in anger, yet still in disbelief. Perhaps after 14 months in this House my disbelief should be tempered with knowledge of the activity and agenda of the other side.
I speak particularly as a member from the beleaguered region of Atlantic Canada. I listened today, and I listened proudly, to the words of my colleagues from Lambton-Middlesex, from Miramichi and from Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte, as well as others who spoke eloquently and long on the subject of this government's particular agenda.
I listened and I listened proudly knowing that my colleagues speak out for all regions this country which are suffering at the hands of this government. But, as an Atlantic Canadian, I suppose you can call this a special pleading because I think there is not another region that suffers quite so badly at the hands of this government.
We have seen it day after day in this House, in bill after bill, in policy after policy. The Atlantic fishery is in crisis, no matter what the right hon. Prime Minister might say. VIA Rail has been cut to pieces. Atlantic Canadian students, seniors and the sick are unable to depend on the transportation lifeline that they have relied on for so many years. We have seen another nail in the coffin of our economy.
I listened with interest to the comment of the minister, who appears to have gone somewhere, regarding the so-called wondrous gifts of ACOA. Those of us in Atlantic Canada, those of us who sit here and represent our fellow Atlantic Canadians, know the myth of that kind of talk. As my colleague from Miramichi said, we will not forget. We will remember.
Last June, many of the same people who rose today to speak on the issue of the at and east subsidy rose then as well to talk about the devastation the passage of this bill will create in our region. We talked about it then because of the effective date in the legislation, the fact that before the bill had been presented to this House the word was already out in the Atlantic and elsewhere that
July 16 would be the effective date of the cancellation of the subsidy.
It is more than just a coincidence. It is the fulfilment of yet another piece of the agenda of this government. Those of us duly elected by our people from coast to coast are irrelevant to the workings of this government. The subsidy is cancelled on July 16 and the bill comes into this House on February 12-seven months later. It is not only not good enough. It is an insult to the people who represent Canadians on both sides of this Chamber.
My colleague from Kingston and the Islands asked my colleague from Miramichi what the farmers in Atlantic Canada think of the cancellation of this subsidy. The hon. member for Miramichi said that they thought it was disastrous. I think that he was being kind. In truth the response, should you ask Atlantic Canadian farmers what they think of the cancellation of the at and east, is simply unparliamentary. I cannot tell you what that response is but I can leave it to the imagination. I hope the imaginations of my friends opposite are fairly vivid. Atlantic Canadian farmers are in distress. They are going to be in more distress because of the cost of feed.
I represent a riding that is urban. There are no agricultural holdings in my riding, but every Atlantic Canadian suffers when one sector of the economy is attacked. When every sector of our economy is under attack, as it has been since the disastrous budget of 1989, then all Atlantic Canadians, urban or rural in whatever jobs they have left, are in difficulty and will continue to be in difficulty.
I go back to the purpose of the program. According to the then Minister of Transport, the Liberal Minister of Transport, the Hon. J. W. Pickersgill, in 1966 there were two major purposes for the at and east. The first was to ensure that eastern Canadian ports could compete with U.S. ports and to enable the ports of Halifax and Saint John to compete with Montreal and other St. Lawrence River ports.
The cancellation of this subsidy is a microcosm for the long-term policies of this government vis-a-vis our nation. To ensure that eastern Canadian ports could compete with U.S. ports, I am afraid we have seen over the last 14 months just how keen this government is to
February 12, 1990

have any industry in this country compete too heavily with our American friends.
I am afraid that when it comes to a choice between struggling industry and workers on the east coast of Canada and American business, in the minds of this government American business will win out. There are many benefits to this program.
The program has caused the railways to earn gross revenues averaging $33.5 million over the period from 1971 to 1981. Georgian Bay ports and transfer elevators earned revenue averaging $1.4 million per year and maintained about 75 jobs as a result of the program. Halifax and Saint John earned revenues averaging $1.6 million per year and maintained about 85 jobs.
That may not sound like a lot but believe me in the Atlantic Canadian economy it is major and important. The loss of those jobs and others relating to this subsidy will cut and cut deeply into a section of the country that is already battered and bleeding.
In anticipation of what we will be receiving at the hands of the government on the night of February 20, when the new budget comes down, some of us in Atlantic Canada have looked at each other and said: "Well, maybe we do not have a lot to fear". The reason we may not have a lot to fear is because there is practically nothing left that can be taken away from us, unless the government decides to fire bomb our cities, which may be the next step. I should probably not issue that challenge; God knows what they might come up with.
The milling industry benefits significantly from the subsidy program without which the export flour trade might become extinct. Between 1976 and 1985 the flour industry exported 406,308 tonnes on average annually under the program. Approximately 70 per cent of the flour shipped for export was milled in eastern Canada.
In 1985 the industry received about $16 million in subsidy payments compared to about $9.7 million in 1976.
Much of the decrease in Canadian export flour trade can be attributed to the significant market share captured by the EEC. The EEC members have been heavily subsidized under the common agricultural policy. This financial assistance has enabled them to increase their share of the world flour market from about 8 per cent in 1970-71 to 58 per cent in 1984-85. Yet this government
Government Orders
has something against subsidies that might do the same thing for eastern Canadian industries and might see us add a little to a much beleaguered economic situation.
Grain producers in eastern and western Canada benefit through freight cost savings and shipments made under the program and the realization of higher average returns by spreading out marketing quantities of grain throughout the year. This is particularly true of Ontario grain producers.
The Ontario Wheat Producers Marketing Board exports about 450,000 tonnes to 600,000 tonnes of grain, of which about 150,000 tonnes move under the at and east subsidy program. The existence of the Georgian Bay-Great Lakes transfer elevator facilities enable Ontario producers to store their crop and market it over an extended period of time, thereby yielding producers the best average return.
The railways, CN and CP, received the subsidy for the transportation of grain and flour at the frozen rate. They also gain from the handling of grain at railway owned and/or operated elevators in Georgian Bay and Saint John, New Brunswick. In 1985 the railways received average subsidies of $23.40 per tonne for grain and $63.58 per tonne for flour. As noted earlier, a number of old Ontario elevators and the elevators in Halifax and Saint John owe their existence to the at and east subsidy.
It is conceivable the Port McNicoll, Midland and Owen Sound would not exist as transfer facilities without the subsidy. The same is absolutely true of the maritime elevators. Those maritime elevators, and the one I know most particularly, the one in Halifax, mark a part of our skyline and they show us in the city of Halifax that people are working. This ideal is becoming less and less true as we drive around Atlantic Canada. This ideal has become untrue for the people of Lockeport. It has become much less true for the people of Canso. It has never been true since this government came in for the people of Cape Breton, in spite of the words of the hon. minister.
Bay port elevators provide maritime elevators with most of their at and east grain traffic. This traffic, subsidized by the at and east, accounts for 95 per cent of total receipts at Saint John and 70 per cent of total receipts at Halifax. We have been discussing, debating,

February 12, 1990
Government Orders
complaining and asking the government to change its mind about this for over a year. There has been no response.
It is interesting. It is not all cakes and ale on the Conservative side of the fence as far as this goes. There are even some Conservative members who are not terribly happy about this decision. Even an hon. Tory, the member for Annapolis Valley-Hants, is on record as supporting offsets to help grain growers in the region. I think it would be interesting to know how he really feels about the cancellation of the at and east subsidy.
Halifax is a city that depends on its ports. The grain elevators, the activity produced by the grain elevators, and the jobs created thereto are a part of the relative economic health of the city of Halifax. I say "relative" because it is relative to the ill health of the rest of the region. That ill health in the rest of the region has been caused by the poisoned dart of government policy.
There is no particular reason, other than a government devoted to a Canada that does not exist outside the very central part of our geography, to see our regions die, and yet they are dying. They are dying from a lack of interest. They are dying from an interest that can only be described as poisonous and that can only be described as anti the best interests of large numbers of Canadian citizens.
If the regional elevators lose the grain exports from the at and east subsidy and somehow on their other business manage to remain open, $14.4 million in economic activity will be lost. But, if both regional elevators shut down, loss of economic activity will be in excess of $27 million. Local livestock and poultry industries in the maritimes face a tremendous disadvantage in terms of feed costs versus the costs in central Canada.
Again, another hit below the belt. Another damaging blow to a small but viable industry in the Atlantic region. It almost gets to the point where Atlantic Canadians look around and say: "What did we do to deserve this?". Some may respond that what Atlantic Canadians did to deserve this was send too many people to this Chamber, to sit on my side of the House. I look at my colleagues from Atlantic Canada who sit on your side of the House. I look at the member for South Shore, possibly the second most beleaguered riding in Canada, which is
home to Lockeport and home to Barrington and used to be home to a VIA Rail route.
I look at the member for Cumberland-Colchester. I look at the member for Halifax West and I look at the Minister from Central Nova, and I want to say to them: "How can you live with this specific policy that points a gun at the heart of your region, and daily sees the people you represent, your fellow Nova Scotians, losing their jobs, losing their livelihood, but worst of all, losing their hope".
That is the ultimate terror and the ultimate disgrace of the policy of this government, of this anti-national government that looks at people in a region and says that because they live in the Atlantic, or because they live in the north, or because they live in the west, they are not full-fledged Canadians and do not deserve the same benefits that other Canadians enjoy. They do not have a right to stay in their towns and villages and cities to bring up their children and buy their houses and live a decent Canadian standard of living.
I will never ever forget sitting in Halifax with the committee on the UI changes. I heard an hon. member opposite say to the President of Federation acadienne de Nouvelle-Ecosse that if young Acadian Nova Scotians could not find jobs, they had an easy option. They could move or they could starve. Well, we do not accept that. We do not accept it in Atlantic Canada and we will not accept it. This government had better realize it now, and realize it fast.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext: She is threatening us now.

Yes, she is threatening, Bill. Indeed, there are a lot of other people who are threatening, right behind me. There are 800,000 people in the province of Nova Scotia. There are 500,000 plus in the province of New Brunswick. There are 150,000 in Prince Edward Island. Small, I admit. But we are there and we are vocal. The members who have been elected to represent those people will continue to be vocal.
You can make your policies. You can practise your scorched earth policy, your search and destroy missions on the Atlantic. But we survive. We survived John Diefenbaker, and we will survive you. The sooner you are aware of that and the sooner you start thinking about what that is going to mean for you and all your friends in 1992, I think the happier you may be. Believe me, we
February 12, 1990

were here before you got here and we will be here long after you have gone.
Hear, hear!
We are tough.
You had better find a leader.

My dear, we are burdened with a plethora of leaders. You should only be so lucky.
In answer to this obvious desire to change the subject by my less than learned colleagues across the floor, may I merely state that it is only typical of the tunnel vision of my hon. colleagues that they cannot see the forest for the trees.
However, back to the issue at hand, the issue of the at and east. The cancellation of the subsidy is a disgrace and it is one that will long, long be remembered.
I move:
That the motion be amended by deleting all the words after the
word "that" and substituting the following therefor:
That Bill C-26, an Act to amend the Railway Act (grain and flour subsidies), be not now read a second time, but that it be read a second time this day six months hence.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 38 is deemed to have been moved.

Mr. Speaker, on December 13, 1989, I asked the Minister of Employment and Immigration whether she would immediately discontinue the Immigrant Investors Program which allows wealthy people to buy their way into Canada by investing $250,000 or, in the case of the prairie provinces or the maritimes, $150,000. I also asked whether she would take action to ensure fairness in Canada's immigration policy.
The success of this buy-a-passport program is questionable. There are many reports of investors losing their money in government-sanctioned immigrant investor funds. At least five such funds in B.C., including three
Adjournment Debate
that were controlled by the Merbanco Group of Calgary, Pinetree Software Canada and New Canada have been called failures. Investors who had deposited money in EdmontAsia Capital Corporation, an Alberta-based investment fund that was also managed by the Merbanco Group, have been told that at least half of their money was gone. The failure of these government-sanctioned immigrant investor funds not only gives Canada a bad name, it also gives bad publicity to other investment funds which are reputable.
There are also complaints that the money from some of these immigrant investor funds are not used for economic development and job creation. Money invested in Pinetree Software Canada has been tucked away in a trust company collecting interest. In the meantime the company has been declared a failure. The Canadian Maple Leaf Fund has invested $581,000 in real estate development in Whistler. Yet, under federal guidelines this immigrant investor money cannot be used for real estate ventures. These kinds of investments do not contribute to creating permanent jobs or economic wealth which might have been a value of this program.
Everyone knows that this program is out of control. Nobody knows how much money has been properly invested, how much money sits collecting interest and how much money has been lost. Until last August this program was not even monitored by the government.
I oppose the business immigration program in principle. It creates two classes of immigrants, an elite group and a non-elite group. It allows wealthy people to buy their way into Canada while those who are not wealthy find it very difficult to immigrate. Many persons are excluded. I know many in my riding who would be good Canadian citizens, bringing energy and skills and hard work, but they are excluded because they cannot make enough points or do not have enough capital to buy their way in. Incidentally, the new fees for sponsors are not helping either. Many sponsoring relatives work at several low-paying jobs to try to bring relatives over and they are very hurt by long delays and frequent refusals, while others can buy their way in in very short time.
Business immigrants are given second highest priority in processing after the family class immigrants and refugees. They only need to receive 25 points to have their applications approved while 70 points is normally required by other immigrants. It is proof that money is power according to this government, it allows people to buy-their way into Canada. It also gives the wrong

February 12, 1990
Adjournment Debate
message to newcomers about Canadian values which I had hoped would be based on fairness and equality.
There is also a huge backlog of refugee claimants here in Canada who are still waiting for the decision as to whether or not they are going to be allowed to stay as landed immigrants. At the end of 1988 there were over 107,000 in this backlog, approximately 100,000 of whom had not even been given the initial interview. This is our new streamlined procedure.
In 1989, when the new refugee determination system was implemented, the government said there would be no further backlogs, yet 7,000 of the latest claimants are in a new backlog still waiting for a decision. Under the new system refugee claimants have had to wait up to four months for the credible basis hearing, which is only the second stage in the refugee determination process. What does the government intend to do to expedite this process?
We must also give refugee claimants work visas and language training while they are waiting so that they will have some security, and their children must have schooling.
Around the world thousands of refugees wait in refugee camps for a country to accept them, particularly in southeast Asian countries and in Hong Kong. There are many living in overcrowded living quarters with poor sanitary facilities where contagious diseases and outbreaks of violence are common. The daily arrival of more refugees is causing great strain on the limited facilities, particularly in Hong Kong, which is a very small place. And yet, while Canada openly criticizes the Hong Kong decision to repatriate these refugees, we have not opened our doors to take them in order to both help the refugees and alleviate the situation in Hong Kong.
New Democrats believe in a fairer immigration policy which considers family reunification as a top priority. In many cultures "family" has a broad meaning. It includes an extended family and this should be considered in our immigration policy. In a multicultural Canada we believe
the family should include extended family members in the family unit.
Immigrants in Canada face a very difficult time adjusting to their new environment and to the values of a new society, and yet the government is cutting back on the settlement language program. This is a good program but because of the lack of continuity in funding, it results in an ineffective program for many, women in particular. That should be changed.
We also have objected many times to the cut-backs in the Citizen Instruction in Language Training program, which will be cut out entirely by this government. This means that newcomers, particularly women and people who are not in the workforce, will not be able to get the kind of settlement services which they need.
I call on the minister once again to review and withdraw the Immigrant Investor Program and to reinstate the CILT program so that entry to Canada will be fair and equitable and new Canadians will have the assistance they need to settle quickly in a multicultural Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to expand upon the reply given by the hon. Minister of Employment and Immigration to the hon. member for Vancouver East on December 13 concerning the Immigrant Investor Program.
In 1989, investor immigrants, their spouses and dependents accounted for 1.1 per cent of total immigration. Since its introduction in January 1986, approximately 3,000 investor immigrants, including spouses and dependents, have been granted landing. In that same period, the total immigration has exceeded 550,000 people.
Investor immigrants increase investment funds available for small and medium-sized businesses across Canada. The investor program itself is supported by all provinces and provides a meaningful and growing support tool to enhance regional and professional economic development in Canada. Immigrant investors' funds are intended primarily to increase and maintain Canadian employment. Nevertheless, the investor program is relatively new and has to be refined further. The govern-
February 12, 1990

ment has recognized this and has implemented measures to improve the administration of this program.
For example, on May 2, 1989, the minister announced the creation of the Business Advisory Committee to advise the minister on issues relating to business immigration. A business immigration unit has been established within Employment and Immigration Canada to concentrate on the effective operation of this program. An investor monitoring system has been developed and new regulations have been put in place. All of this has taken place in the context of ongoing negotiation and co-operation with the provinces.
Preliminary reports indicate that since 1986 this program has produced or maintained over 11,000 Canadian jobs with more to come. This is a program which not only creates jobs, but brings people, skills and capital to all parts of Canada. In short, the investor program benefits all regions of Canada. It is the intention of the government to continue working with its provincial partners to improve the program and to continue to attract investor immigrants to this country.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question this evening relates to an article that appeared in The Globe and Mail on November 29 of last year. I asked a question in the House on that same date and I will refer to that in a moment to refresh Your Honour's memory of the occasion.
The article of November 29 read in part as follows:
Internal Conservative Party documents reveal a proposal that, in certain circumstances, Tory fundraisers would remind potential corporate donors of federal government contracts they have received.
But documents obtained by The Globe and Mail show that there were detailed plans within the Progressive Conservative Canada Fund to set up a computerized system in which the file on each corporate donor would include a list of the number of government contracts, grants or policies that have benefited that corporation.
The Globe and Mail reporters did some interviews. They interviewed one Nicolas Locke, executive director of the PC Canada Fund. The article goes on:
Adjournment Debate
Nicolas Locke, executive director of the PC Canada Fund, the party's fundraising arm, confirmed in an interview last week that the party has computerized files on each corporate donor, and that the files were updated in 1986 after an internal review.
But Mr. Locke denied that the files contain information about government contracts, grants or policies beneficial to the company-
Mr. Locke also strongly denied that party fundraisers ever mention government contracts or grants when they discuss a donation with a donor or prospective donor.
"They're clearly directed not to do that," he said. "Some people in this world have gotten into trouble doing things like that, but they have not been associated with the PC Canada Fund."
Well, as a footnote, Mr. Speaker, they certainly were not but they were clearly associated with the PC Party of this country.
Then he went on:
Mr. Locke said that he suspects that soliciting donations from donors by reminding them of government business they have received would be not only improper but possibly illegal.
Imagine. He really thought about that one before he spoke. Then he went on:
"Our canvassers are told in no uncertain terms not to get involved in that sort of thing," he said. "If anybody started soliciting that way, they'd be drummed out."
Well, we know what happened to some of the cabinet ministers. Ten of them have been drummed out and we know that two of the Conservative back-benchers have been accused of illegal activities in connection with fundraising. One has been convicted and one is currently facing a host of charges.
We have evidence of impropriety in the Oerlikon land deals that seem to have been forgotten. While the story in The Globe and Mail may be of some interest, it only touches the tip of the iceberg. We can see how big the iceberg is when we look later in the story. In the third column it says:
Last year, the Conservatives dramatically outstripped the two major parties in raising money from the business community, collecting $14.3 million in corporate donations, compared to $8.4 million collected by the Liberals and $262,000 received by the New Democrats, according to public election records.
I would not want to suggest that the New Democratic Party is immune to this sort of thing because, after all, their fundraising is done through the unions and they pay for that in the way they are required to follow the dictates of the union bosses. We hear about that in the

Adjournment Debate
spats that arise between the government members and the New Democrats from time to time in the House.
As a result of all this I put a question to the Deputy Prime Minister on November 29.1 asked him if he would tell the House whether in fact the government sent lists of persons who received government contracts to anybody, and specifically to the PC Canada Fund. The Deputy Prime Minister, in his first answer, said that I was referring to a discredited stoiy and I need not worry about it. He did not answer my question. I then asked him if he would tell us whether he would instruct his bagmen to appear before the Election Reform Commission that he has established to reveal their practices and their lists. He sloughed off the question by saying, as reported at page 6374 of Hansard:
-if the hon. member wants to make reference to the commission about who should appear or who should not appear, he can make that representation directly to the commission.
It is my submission, first, that the Deputy Prime Minister has an obligation to answer my question, and I hope when we hear from the parliamentary secretary, although I am sure he is reluctant to get to his feet on this one, that he will tell us that these lists are not forwarded to the PC Canada Fund and that there are in fact no such lists.
But I suspect that there are such lists and I would like to know to whom they are made available. Certainly the lists could be compiled from answers we can put on the Order Paper in this House and certainly they come out in press releases. I think that members of this House should know whether in fact these lists are prepared by the government and forwarded to the PC Canada Fund so they can be put on this computer.
If they are, it supports the story in The Globe and Mad. It gives evidence of potential risk of wrong-doing and I think we ought to take steps to see that that sort of risk is minimized.
After ten resignations from the cabinet, and I can think of only two prosecutions under the Criminal Code for offences relating to fundraising, I think it is time that the government took stern measures, and I think that is putting it mildly, to ensure that this kind of conduct does not continue.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Employment and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Employment and Immigration
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member is a member of the second oldest profession in the world, that is why they are sometimes called solicitors. That is what he was going through today.
I believe the hon. member's question stems from newspaper articles which appeared in late November of last year. Those articles referred to a draft report dating back to 1986, which report was never adopted. Indeed, I understand that the lists of government contracts are not and never have been used by PC Canada Fund. I hope that puts the matter to rest.
The hon. member has also raised questions with respect to the Royal Commission on Electoral Reform and Party Finance. The government's intention to establish this commission of inquiry was announced in the Speech from the Throne to open the second session of the Thirty-fourth Parliament on November 15, 1989. The Prime Minister announced the establishment of a commission to inquire into and report on the appropriate principles and process that should govern the election of members of the House of Commons and the financing of political parties and candidates' campaigns.
The Prime Minister further indicated that this study would include an examination of the practices, procedures and legislation in Canada; the means by which which political parties should be funded, the provision of the funds to the political parties from any source and the limits of such funding and the uses to which such funds ought or ought not be put; and the qualification of electors and the compiling of voters' lists, including the advisability of the establishment of a permanent voters' list.
I understand that in mid-January the chairman of the commission, Mr. Pierre Lortie, wrote to various people, including all members of this House, inviting them to participate at public hearings. I am sure the hon. member received the letter as I did. I hope he will make his submission. In addition, public notices were published in newspapers across the country requesting all those who wish to express an opinion to provide relevant information and to submit a written brief to the commission by March 9, 1990.
I understand that the commission plans to begin public hearings in the spring. The government has long recognized the need to amend and improve our electoral laws. Indeed, many important amendments were introduced in the last Parliament in Bill C-79. Unfortunately, the
February 12, 1990

government was not able to secure the co-operation of the Liberal and New Democratic parties to allow passage of even those portions of the bill to which all parties had agreed.
The government hopes that the important work undertaken by the commission will help develop a consensus on many complex issues. The commission is uniquely qualified to provide advice on the principles and the process that governs elected representatives and their respective political parties. The government looks forward to receiving that advice.

Mr. Speaker, when I rose on December 8 in this House, the nation was stunned and sorrowing because of the horrific slaying of the young women students in Montreal.
At that time I asked the Prime Minister a series of questions, questions to which he and the Minister of Employment and Immigration made some response. My questions were simple. First, I asked the Prime Minister whether he would agree to the appointment of a joint House of Commons and Senate committee to seek solutions to the all-pervasive problem of violence against women in Canada.
Second, I asked whether the Prime Minister intended to consult with representatives of women's groups in order to take advantage of their particular expertise and wipe out violence against women.
Third, I asked whether the Prime Minister would undertake to restore funding to the women's programs, at least those dealing with violence against women that were slashed by 15 per cent.
At that time the Prime Minister and the Minister of Employment and Immigration who, of course, as we all know, is also the minister responsible for the status of women, made a commendable effort to demonstrate how appalled this government was by the events in Montreal.
The Prime Minister stressed that he had met the students from the University of Montreal and that this government is using any number of means to wipe out
Adjournment Debate
such violence. Unfortunately, this is just another example of how words come more cheaply than actions.
The depth of the problem has not lessened simply because time has passed since the massacre in Montreal. However, this government's commitment to eradicating violence against women has not only lessened, it makes most of us think that it is non-existent.
The fact remains that no joint House of Commons and Senate committee has been appointed. Women's programs across the board have been slashed by 15 per cent and, if the Prime Minister has met on any form of official basis with groups committed to erasing violence against women, he certainly has not told us about it. I suspect that if he had, he would have.
What will it take for this government to finally open its eyes and recognize that it must do something. Yes, the situation in Montreal was horrific because of the circumstances and the number of young women who died. But every day in Canada women are beaten, women are abused, and women die. Action is needed. Action is needed now. It is not enough just to recognize that the problem exists. We all recognize that the problem exists. The time has come to do something, to say something, and to act.
On one hand the Prime Minister claims that this is one of the most serious problems in our society, but it seems that this is the extent to which the Prime Minister is prepared to go. Programs are underfunded. Women's groups have not been called upon to assist in the creation of a strategy to remedy this situation and, most absurd, the Prime Minister has not utilized the resources at his disposal to appoint a House of Commons and Senate committee which could hear the immediate responses of many groups across this country with good ideas as to how we stem the tide of violence against women.
So what do we have? We have a government that is committed to inaction. I do not for a moment suggest that the horrific events that occurred in Montreal and the day-to-day violence against women do not touch members on the government side as much as they touch members on the opposition side. But I do suggest that there does not seem to be a political will on the other side to act.
I have asked questions in this House before, relating to the special initiatives program to stem the tide of violence against women, as it pertains to transition houses. The answer I get is that less than a quarter of the money has been spent. What do I hear from women's groups across Canada involved in transition houses? I

February 12, 1990
Adjournment Debate
hear that when they contact the federal government they do not get a response, they do not hear, they do not know how to go about accessing the money that was promised over 18 months ago.
I certainly hope that the hon. parliamentary secretary has some good news for us on this issue. It is time for the government to act and make a legitimate effort to end violence against women. The fact of the matter is that if he does not act, then the Prime Minister does not see this as one of the most serious problems in our society.
Fifty-two per cent of the population of this country has reason to fear more than the other 48 per cent of the population of this country. It is wrong. We all know it. But it does no good to stand in this House and pontificate. It does no good to say yes, we care, if we do not act, and action costs money. The only thing that is going to save the lives and the sanity and the dignity of Canadian women who are daily in jeopardy is government action and government money and it has to start now.

speakeroldname: Mrs. Lise Bourgault (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members on both sides of the House have rightly expressed their indignation about the tragic events that occurred last December. In our efforts to understand what lay behind the horrifying massacre of 14 young women at the University of Montreal, we have tried to find reasons and explanations for the senseless and inexplicable act of a profoundly disturbed individual. Marc Lepine acted alone. However, his actions have shown to what extent violence can permeate society.
Our government is now making a concerted effort to reduce the manifestations of this violence. Through measures announced last year to fight family violences,
$40 million is being spent on protection, treatment and prevention. The federal government is also working very closely with the provinces and the non-governmental sector on developing a comprehensive national strategy to fight family violence in this country. In fact, the forum on family violence held last June was a veiy important part of this process, as the hon. member should know. We expect to be able to announce a national strategy next spring. I hope it will be a satisfactory response to her request that we create a special joint committee of the House and the Senate, which I don't think would be the answer and would not produce the results this forum will provide for the government and, of course, for women and children who are victims of violence.
I would also like to recall that in 1987, this government passed legislation to deal with child sexual abuse. We will be talking about this very shortly.
Mr. Speaker, violence is not some impersonal force like wind or rain. Violence exists because people are capable of violence. Governments cannot legislate attitudes. However, we can introduce programs and take measures that promote changes in attitude. That is what we have done with our measures to combat violence, and that is why many of these measures support the efforts deployed by non-governmental organizations to improve people's perceptions and relationships with each other.
Mr. Speaker, we all, and I am sure the hon. member will agree, want to put an end to violence towards women, children and the most vulnerable in our society. It is the most earnest wish of this government and your humble servant.
